topic_summaries.UK Energy Mix and Net Zero Targets:
• BBC and The Guardian frame the £12bn offshore wind investment and Energy Independence Bill as central to the UK's net zero journey, while GB News emphasises grid vulnerability during low-wind periods and uses gas dependency to question renewable reliability
• GB News consistently adopts a sceptical or critical framing — highlighting landlord fines, North Sea drilling bans, and taxpayer costs — contrasting with the Evening Standard and Guardian, which present the same wind investment and Burnham's COP31 preparations more favourably
• BBC uniquely surfaces the public consent challenge, with Fahnbulleh acknowledging net zero is "under pressure" amid rising living costs, a tension the Mirror largely sidesteps in favour of celebrity climate coverage (Prince William/Earthshot)
topic_summaries.Cop31 Climate Summit:
• The Guardian dominates coverage with broad framing across urgency, geopolitics, and criticism — highlighting US absence, fossil fuel industry lobbying, Australian contradictions, and climate finance delays; BBC focuses more narrowly on scientific benchmarks like record temperatures and the 1.5C threshold.

• Channel 4 News takes an ironic angle, framing Trump's Iran war as an accidental green energy catalyst via soaring fuel prices — a contrast to The Guardian and Independent's more straightforward treatment of US obstruction.

• The Independent emphasises lived experience and emotional stakes — Britain's current heatwaves, extreme heat reshaping climate debates — while The Guardian leans more toward institutional and diplomatic process scrutiny.
topic_summaries.Solar and Renewable Energy Uptake:
• The i focuses on personal, consumer-level benefits of plug-in solar panels, framing renewable uptake as an accessible, money-saving choice for ordinary people

• The Independent similarly emphasises household financial benefits and practical guidance around solar grants, while GB News highlights Labour rejecting a large solar farm, framing renewable expansion as politically contested

• The Guardian's two pieces look beyond the UK, covering US legislative and electoral politics around clean energy, framing renewables within broader affordability and policy debates
topic_summaries.El Niño: Impacts and Outlook:
• BBC and The Guardian lead with human impact — flooding in Kenya, crop damage in Latin America, storm devastation in East Asia — while Daily Mail emphasises record-breaking climate statistics and future CO2 projections
• Daily Mail offers the most varied framing, covering both alarming consequences ("supercharging the climate crisis") and a counterintuitive positive angle (fewer cold-related deaths)
• Evening Standard focuses narrowly on domestic economic consequences for UK consumers; GB News provides no substantive El Niño coverage in the available source text
topic_summaries.UK Air Pollution Alerts:
• Evening Standard leads coverage with real-time London-specific alerts, mapping borough-level risk and citing Imperial College forecasters; GB News frames the same fog-related pollution as a broader Britain-wide warning
• Metro focuses on Bonfire Night fireworks as the pollution trigger, framing it as a "code red" event distinct from the fog narrative dominating other outlets
• The Independent's articles stray off-topic to Delhi's air pollution; BBC's included article covers sewage rather than air pollution alerts — neither directly addresses the UK alert story
topic_summaries.Electric Vehicles and Green Transport Po:
• GB News and The Guardian both cover Andy Burnham's response to potential EV target changes, but GB News frames it as a "U-turn" risk while The Guardian presents Burnham's own dismissal of reports as "speculation"

• The i takes multiple critical angles on EVs — cybersecurity vulnerabilities, rising costs if targets are watered down, and rural impracticality — while The Guardian's Monbiot frames industry resistance as deliberate lobbying and political cowardice

• Daily Mail focuses on a surveillance framing around road tax and satnav tracking, distinct from other outlets' coverage of the broader EV mandate debate
topic_summaries.Polar Vortex Winter Weather Threat:
• Metro leads coverage with urgent, record-breaking framing — describing the polar vortex as "dangerous and unprecedented" and citing Met Office warnings of earliest-ever Sudden Stratospheric Warming
• The Mirror teases a mystery "most concerning" impact beyond snow or climate change, using sensational hooks without revealing detail in the excerpt
• The Guardian's provided articles do not cover the polar vortex topic, instead focusing on heat exhaustion and bird flu — suggesting markedly different editorial priorities

articles.jina_text:
Guterres launches into a plea for accelerated action to cut emissions and takes direct aim at the fossil fuel industry. The UN chief has already called on countries to push forward a phase out of fossil fuels, rather than merely hinting at it, here at Cop.


UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres makes his plea to the leaders summit at Cop31. Photograph: Dogukan Keskinkilic/Anadolu/Getty Images
“The case for fossil fuels is collapsing,” he said. “Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs. And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do.”
“It’s time to kick the habit – and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said. Guterres likes a good pun and one of his final climate speeches has a decent one: “It’s make or bake time.”

Key events

'The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do.' - UN chief

5h ago

7h ago
Day 3 of Cop31 kicks off


Samia Suluhu Hassan, president of Tanzania, has warned that climate-related shocks are estimated to cost up to 2-3% of her country’s GDP each year. She’s called for better climate finance and more transparent carbon markets.
She’s followed by Nikos Christodoulides, president of Cyprus, who has touted his nation’s role in helping the wider Mediterranean and Middle East region. He has also warned against divisions in our fight against global warming. “Climate change transcends politics and does not recognise borders.”


As you may be sick of hearing from me already on this blog, I think the Cop31 theme tune “Let’s Cop” is a bit of a catchy banger.
“Bring down the heat make it drop.” 
 “One world, one call, let’s Cop.”
But there may be a cruel twist that might quell my enthusiasm. First, have a listen.



The Cop31 theme song, “Let’s Cop”.
One of my Australian reporter colleagues here spent many years as a tech reporter and thought she smelt the whiff of AI. More than one AI detector, she said, suggested she might be right.
So I asked the Turkish hosts if “Let’s Cop” might be AI slop (this isn’t exactly how I put it and, to be fair, I don’t think it is slop but the rhyme as too good to resist). Here’s what they said:
“The song’s lyrics and composition were created by a professional artist, with AI technology used solely to assist with the vocals.”
Did that mean the singing voice and the instruments were AI?
“The song’s melody and lyrics was written by a professional musician, while AI tools were used in the composition and production process.”
Make of that what you will. I now hate that I like it.

We’ve now heard from Shavkat Mirziyoyev, from Uzbekistan, who has described safeguarding our planet as “a sacred responsibility we all share”.
He was followed by an unscheduled intervention from a representative from Azerbaijan, the host of Cop29, who highlighted some of the achievements from the climate summit in Baku two years ago.
Next up is Tanzania.

By emphasizing the direct impacts of extreme heat on communities and families, campaigners hope to drive greater government accountability and public advocacy.
For Turkey, the Mediterranean host of the Cop31 conference, episodes of extreme heat are among the most obvious experiences of the climate crisis. The country faced an estimated 642.9 million working hours lost in 2024 due to heat stress, according to the Cop presidency – while a record temperature of 50.5C recorded in 2025 coincided with devastating wildfires that burned some 154,000 hectares.

The country is far from alone in facing increasingly dangerous heat, with much of the world facing soaring temperatures in 2026, and a number of heatwaves. Temperature records fell across European countries in this summer, with the UK notably experiencing five heatwaves. articles.jina_text:
Anthony Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on climate change in a historic speech to the UN’s climate summit, but one which failed to mention the fossil fuels driving the crisis.
The Australia prime minister landed in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya on Wednesday morning where the Cop31 talks are being presided over by his climate change minister, Chris Bowen, but hosted by Turkey.







Developing countries in limbo as rich nations delay new climate finance plans

Read more
Only moments before Albanese spoke, on the same stage the UN secretary general Antonio Guterres said unambiguously that keeping the 1.5C temperature goal alive “means no new coal”.
In a packed conference room, Turkey put on an opening ceremony of whirling traditional dancers, booming music and a film shot around the world with characters saying “We need to talk”.
“This is an historic moment for my country,” said Albanese, adding Australia was “proud to be a leader on climate action.”
“Proud to be a renewable energy leader, creating the clean industries, businesses and jobs of the future. And proud to be here fighting for the interests of our Pacific family,” he said.
Australia had pushed for a role at the climate summit, he said, “because we wanted to speak for the people of the world who need urgent action, including those from our Pacific family”.
Australia is the world’s second largest exporter of coal for burning in power stations and the largest exporter of coal for steelmaking. A fifth of the world’s exported LNG comes from Australia.
Albanese pointed to “significant successes” for the country on climate change, including doubling renewable energy generation in six years that accounted for half of the country’s electricity, and building one of the world’s biggest rooftop solar and battery markets.
Guterres and several countries are pushing for the talks to progress a proposal from last year’s Cop hosts, Brazil, for countries to develop detailed plans to move away from fossil fuels.
Guterres told the conference: “Leaders – and in particular those from developed countries – cannot keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5 degrees.”
He said to keep the globally-agreed goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C within reach, coal power had to fall by at least 75% by 2035.
Unabated coal power – that is, coal generated without safely capturing the carbon dioxide emissions – “must be all but phased out” by 2040, and oil and gas use cut by a third, he said.
“Every government must align its policies, investments and infrastructure plans accordingly. That starts with credible national roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels — protecting workers and communities.
“That means no new coal. No new oil and gas infrastructure that puts 1.5 degrees further out of reach.”

It’s an exciting time for long-haul travel (Picture: Getty Images/Metro)



It’s official. The Guinness World Record for the longest commercial flight by distance has been broken. 

Let’s refresh our memory. In July, a flight departed Melbourne, Australia, and landed in Toulouse, France, just over 24 hours later.

All in, the plane covered a whopping 12,503 nautical miles, flying over Sydney, the Pacific, and the International Date Line, before cruising over London and on to France.

While there were no paying passengers on board — a crew of pilots and engineers locked in for the ride — there soon will be.





Qantas, Australia’s flag carrier, is gearing up to launch Project Sunrise in 2027, designed to take passengers from London to Sydney in just 22 hours.

The route is expected to revolutionise long-haul travel, complete with game-changing features such as a ‘Wellbeing Zone’ and lighting scenes to reduce jet lag.

However, as mere mortals, our bodies aren’t designed to spend such long periods of time in the air, 40,000 feet above sea level. 

So, to understand what actually happens to our bodies on a long-haul flight, Metro spoke with Dr Nikki Ramskill, private GP and founder of The Female Health Doctor. 

24-hour flight? Ready to complete it, mate.

It was part of the flight test campaign for the Airbus A350-1000ULR, developed for Qantas Airways under its ambitious Project Sunrise. 
All in, the plane covered a whopping 12,503 nautical miles, flying over Sydney, the Pacific, and the International Date Line, before cruising over London and on to France. 

 

While there were no paying passengers on board — a crew of pilots and engineers locked in for the ride — there soon will be. 

  
Qantas, Australia’s flag carrier, is gearing up to launch Project Sunrise in 2027, designed to take passengers from London to Sydney in just 22 hours. 

 
The route is expected to revolutionise long-haul travel, complete with game-changing features such as a ‘Wellbeing Zone’ and lighting scenes to reduce jet lag. 
However, as mere mortals, our bodies aren’t designed to spend such long periods of time in the air, 40,000 feet above sea level.  
So, to understand what actually happens to our bodies on a long-haul flight, Metro spoke with Dr Nikki Ramskill, private GP and founder of The Female Health Doctor.  
24-hour flight? Ready to complete it, mate. 
 
   
If you’ve ever travelled on a long-haul flight in economy, you’ll know it’s meant to test us (Picture: Shutterstock / Matej Kastelic) 
What happens to your body on a long-haul flight? 
According to Dr Ramskill, the body goes through different phases as the hours go on.  
During the first four, when you’re sitting for long periods (especially with your knees bent and very little movement), the calf muscles aren’t doing their job to help pump the blood back to the heart. 
‘This means blood can start to pool in the lower legs, which is why you may find your ankles and feet are quite swollen.’ 
Hours 4 to 8 
This is when the cabin environment starts taking its toll. 
‘Aircraft cabins are pressurised, but the pressure is still lower than we’re used to at sea level, which means there’s a slightly lower concentration of oxygen available to the body.’ But again, most healthy people cope with this. 
The air in the cabin is also very dry, which can leave passengers with dry eyes, nasal passages, skin and mouth. 
Elsewhere, ‘cabin pressure changes can cause the gas in the digestive tract to expand, leading to a feeling of bloating, discomfort or being rather gassy.’  

 
Dr Ramskill adds that sitting in one position can also lead to stiffness in the hips, lower back and neck. 

  
Hours 8 to 12 
Fatigue and sleep disruption become more noticeable here, as our natural body clocks start to clash with the environment we’re in. 
‘Our circadian rhythm dictates when we feel sleepy, alert and hungry,’ the GP states. But on an ultra-long-haul flight, you could be having a meal or trying to go to sleep at a time when your body would normally be doing something different.

articles.jina_text:
Gill (not her real name), 43, is a teacher in London. In 2026, during the hottest summer on record, she suffered a seizure after experiencing heat exhaustion while teaching. The heatwave was made worse by the climate crisis.








 
  

The heat has always made me feel anxious and uncomfortable, but this year was different. The temperature was building up as the summer went on and as it was escalating it was becoming more and more frightening.
It was impossible to get any meaningful rest because I couldn’t fall asleep and when I did, I would wake up feeling suffocated because the air was so thick and dry and hot and there was nothing I could do to make myself feel better. Drinking water, using a fan, it didn’t help.
It got to the point where I would wake up feeling like I couldn’t breathe and with this rising sense of panic where I couldn’t really imagine how I was going to get through the day. I felt unsafe.
There was a lot of anxiety among my colleagues too. People were obviously very uncomfortable, they were worried about the kids, worried about themselves.
One day in late June I woke up and I was exhausted and was lacking the motivation that I normally have for work.


View image in fullscreen
Summer weather in Brockwell Park, south London, in August. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PA
I got to work and my classroom was 30C. It used to be the photocopier room but because of demand for space they took the photocopier out. It’s a very small room with no windows. It was never designed to be a classroom, it’s got no ventilation.
No one was really learning and I was dealing with challenging behaviour and as the day went on I started to feel increasingly unwell to the point where I was dizzy and feverish and I had a really bad headache. I felt like I couldn’t concentrate on anything.
I was diagnosed with epilepsy about 20 years ago. It took about a year to get on top of it, but since then it’s not something that affects my life in any way, it’s extremely well controlled. But on this day, I had my first absent seizure since the diagnosis.
The best way to describe it is like pressing pause on the TV remote. I was on my lunch break and there was a pause and then it was like I restarted again a few seconds later.
I went to meet my colleague in reception, and she told me I had a lot of symptoms of heat exhaustion. I was feverish, I felt cold but my skin was really hot to touch, I was unable to regulate my body temperature and was fluctuating between being really hot and really cold.
No matter how much water I was drinking, I was just feeling chronically thirsty. I’ve never experienced anything like this before, it was really scary.


View image in fullscreen
The dried-up mud bed of Hollow Pond in east London in August. Photograph: Yui Mok/PA
I was supposed to be teaching that afternoon, but I was not able to, so I cancelled the lesson and stayed in first aid.

Climate campaigners say private gas power stations for datacentres are unlikely to be temporary and could lock in high emissions for years. Photograph: Anton Gvozdikov/Alamy
View image in fullscreen
Climate campaigners say private gas power stations for datacentres are unlikely to be temporary and could lock in high emissions for years. Photograph: Anton Gvozdikov/Alamy


AI datacentres plan on-site power stations on huge scale despite climate risks, research reveals


181GW of gas-fired capacity proposed for sites in US and Europe because of delays in connecting to national grids, says report




Developers of AI datacentres plan to build on-site climate-destroying gas power stations on a huge scale to meet their energy demands, research reveals.
Datacentres planned across the US, the UK and mainland Europe have proposals to build fossil fuel plants on-site to create 181GW of gas-fired capacity because of delays to connect to national grids, according to the findings. This is almost four times the total peak electricity demand of Great Britain.

The research by BloombergNEF says this “speed to power” will – if the planned rollout happens – emit about 345m metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a year in the US, where 90% of on-site gas-fired power stations are planned. This is equivalent to annual greenhouse gas emissions from about 72.8m fossil fuel cars.


The report was published on Wednesday as global leaders gathered in Turkey for the 31st UN climate summit, where increasing electrification – ideally from clean sources – is a central part of discussions. However, a number of key European leaders, including from France and Germany, will not be at Cop31, instead heading to Dublin where EU leaders will hold their first dedicated AI summit on Friday.
Mark Daly, the head of datacentres and emerging tech at BloombergNEF, said: “The extraordinary economics around AI are making speed to power one of the most important priorities for defining constraints on datacentre developers.
“The climate outcome will depend not only on how much electricity these facilities use, but on how quickly grids can connect them and whether power systems add cleaner generation alongside that demand.”







Activists break into building site of Microsoft datacentre in Amsterdam

Read more
By 2035, the electricity demand of AI datacentres was predicted to almost quadruple to 2,354 terawatt-hours – equivalent to 7% of global electricity demand – the report said.
AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cool equipment, and to run facility systems.


Daly said while the developers of the future datacentres claimed their gas-fired power supplies would be temporary while they waited for grid connections, once they were online, the economics could encourage them to continue generating energy, creating a longer-term fossil-fuel lock-in risk.
The report said ensuring new datacentres were connected to the grid was the more sustainable option. Fas

Motorists thinking of buying an electric car risk losing hefty discounts unless they act sooner rather than later.



The cost of an electric vehicle (EV) – including second hand cars and hybrids – is set to rise significantly as it is likely that mandated sales targets for manufacturers will be watered down.



EV makers currently offer discounts of several thousand pounds on cars and SUVs – the average discount last year was £2,800 – in order to meet the targets.



These discounts could take a significant cut if manufacturers are not under so much pressure to sell their stock, experts say. 



And, separately, if the Government decides to align with EU tariffs on Chinese EVs as part of efforts to get closer to Europe, it could add £12,600 to the cost of a Chinese model priced at £30,000. EVs produced in China are typically among some of the cheapest on the market.

articles.jina_text:
The cost of an electric vehicle (EV) – including second hand cars and hybrids – is set to rise significantly as it is likely that mandated sales targets for manufacturers will be watered down. 
EV makers currently offer discounts of several thousand pounds on cars and SUVs – the average discount last year was £2,800 – in order to meet the targets.



 
These discounts could take a significant cut if manufacturers are not under so much pressure to sell their stock, experts say.  
And, separately, if the Government decides to align with EU tariffs on Chinese EVs as part of efforts to get closer to Europe, it could add £12,600 to the cost of a Chinese model priced at £30,000. EVs produced in China are typically among some of the cheapest on the market. 
Experts says the lowest price for electric cars is likely to be “right at this moment” and that they expect them to increase from 2027 and beyond.  
Higher prices may lead to fewer sales of new cars which would also feed through into the second-hand market, reducing the supply of vehicles on sale and checking the reduction in prices in this market.



 
The Government’s Zero Emissions Vehicle (ZEV) mandate requires car makers to ensure that 33 per cent of the new cars they sell in 2026 are electric, with the target rising each year to 80 per cent by 2030. Manufacturers that fall short face a £12,000 fine for every vehicle they miss the target by, although there are ways to avoid penalties, such as buying credits from rivals that exceed their targets or offsetting emissions elsewhere in their vehicle fleets. 
Companies that sell more EVs than required can earn extra income by selling these credits to manufacturers struggling to meet the targets. If the Government lowers the EV sales targets as expected, demand for the credits would fall, pushing down their value. That would hit firms such as Tesla and some Chinese brands, which rely heavily on EV sales and credit revenues, potentially leaving them with less scope to cut prices for consumers. 
Ben Westerman, director of policy and advocacy at Electrify Britain – a body which campaigns for electrification – told The i Paper: “Lowering targets will almost certainly contribute to raised electric car prices. Strong targets encourage carmakers to offer discounts on new models. As most people buy second-hand, fewer electric cars now will mean fewer affordable ones in the future.” 
What the discounts look like 
Car firms have been heavily discounting electric vehicles in order to hit the sales targets. For example, the all electric Volvo EX40 – a luxury SUV – is advertised with a £4,250 discount – meaning the £48,860 vehicle is on the road for £44,610. 
For cars priced under £37,000, the government is paying for an EV discount on new all electric cars of £3,750. This can also be combined with a manufacturer’s discount. An MG4 EV is available for £28,995, with a manufacturer’s discount of £1,500.

articles.summary: The cost of electric vehicles in the UK, including second-hand cars and hybrids, is expected to rise significantly in the coming years. Experts warn that if the Government waters down its Zero Emissions Vehicle (ZEV) mandate targets, manufacturers will have less pressure to offer discounts — which averaged £2,800 last year — potentially pushing prices higher from 2027 onwards. Additionally, if the UK aligns with EU tariffs on Chinese EVs, it could add up to £12,600 to the cost of a Chinese-made electric car priced at £30,000.

Full SummaryTurkey's hosting of the Cop31 summit in Antalya faces criticism due to the nation's continued investment in coal and fossil fuels despite its climate pledges. While the government promotes electrification and green industry, the expansion of major coal plants like Afşin-Elbistan has raised significant public health and environmental concerns among local residents.
On the veranda of a small house, Omer coughs as his wife serves up sweet tea and biscuits. The golden glow of late-afternoon sun peaks through nearby foliage and scatters across the floor – an idyllic scene, perhaps, but for a swell of black smoke pooling in the sky over us.
All day – and some say at night, too – emissions chug out in huge columns from alternating chimneys at the nearby Afşin-Elbistan coal plant. It leaves the air all around the surrounding plateau, in Turkey’s southern Kahramanmaraş region, feeling dry and heavy in the mouth and lungs. 
Now in his late fifties, Omer has worked at the vast plant for years, as well as living a stone's throw from it. His brothers also worked there, but in recent years, three have died – two from lung cancer and one of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a progressive lung condition that can be caused or worsened by long-term exposure to coal fumes. 





“I believe working at this plant killed them,” says Omer, pointing his finger towards it in indignation. “And I’m not going to see 65, I know that.”
Another brother is also living with COPD and asthma. According to Omer, his late brothers were between 55 and 61 when they died, and there was no previous history of these illnesses in his family. His father – who was also born in the village – lived to 97.

articles.title: Burnham hails £12bn wind farm investment as he prepares for Cop31 climate talks
articles.raw_rss: The Prime Minister said the investment was a vote of confidence in the UK.
articles.raw_meta: The Prime Minister said the investment was a vote of confidence in the UK.
articles.jina_text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has welcomed a £12 billion investment in wind farms as he prepares to head to the Cop31 climate summit.




Energy company RWE and investment firm KKR have announced the funding which will deliver the Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore wind farms off the Norfolk coast.








The financing includes £1 billion from the state-owned National Wealth Fund.




Prime Minister Andy Burnham has welcomed a £12 billion investment in wind farms as he prepares to head to the Cop31 climate summit.




The wind farms are set to be delivering power by 2030, with construction set to begin early next year.




Mr Burnham said: “This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain.




“It is great news for billpayers because every turbine we put up is power under British control, not at the mercy of events on the other side of the world.




“With coastal communities from Scotland to East Anglia powering Britain’s future, the places that host this energy benefit from the jobs and opportunities that it brings.













“Our National Wealth Fund means that public investment is working alongside private capital to build homegrown energy and bring a return for the taxpayer. Because, for me, a clean energy future is one that brings down bills.”




Mr Burnham will join other world leaders at the United Nations’ Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, where he will deliver a speech on Thursday.









RWE said the Vanguard projects represent one of the UK’s largest offshore wind developments, generating around 2.8 gigawatts, enough to supply three million homes.




The Government said the investment would support more than 2,400 jobs in the construction and operation phases.

Burnham lauds £12bn offshore wind investment as he prepares for climate summit


Package for plan off Norfolk coast revealed as government tries to calm critics after approving Jackdaw gasfield 
 
 
UK politics live – latest updates  




Andy Burnham has hailed a record investment in offshore wind, as the government tries to repair its green credentials after approving the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea.
On Wednesday the government announced a £12bn investment from the German energy company RWE and the US private equity firm KKR, as the prime minister prepares to travel to the Cop31 climate crisis summit in Turkey.

The investment package, which will go towards the creation of the Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore windfarms off the Norfolk coast, is a “vote of confidence for building in Britain”, he said.
“It is great news for bill payers because every turbine we put up is power under British control, not at the mercy of events on the other side of the world.
“With coastal communities from Scotland to East Anglia powering Britain’s future, the places that host this energy benefit from the jobs and opportunities that it brings.”


View image in fullscreen
Andy Burnham has called the investment package a ‘vote of confidence for building in Britain’. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images
The offshore wind projects will also receive £1bn in funding from the state-owned national wealth fund.
The windfarms are set to be providing power by 2030, with construction set to begin early next year. The wind investment is “believed to be the biggest of its kind in UK history”, the government said.
RWE said the Vanguard project represents one of the UK’s largest offshore wind developments, generating about 2.8 gigawatts, enough to supply 3m homes.
It estimated that the construction of the windfarms will create and support 2,300 jobs each year through its supply chain. The windfarms are expected to create a further 100 long-term permanent jobs when they are operational.


The energy company SSE also announced on Wednesday that the latest phase of its major offshore windfarm, Berwick Bank B off the east coast of Scotland, would “support” 2,600 existing jobs.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said investment in offshore wind and clean power was “creating quality jobs and rebuilding industry, while delivering the clean power we need to lower bills and reach net zero”.
She added that Britain was “leading from the front as a renewable energy powerhouse”.

National security of all countries at risk due to climate crisis, UK foreign secretary warns


Exclusive: Ed Miliband says sci-fi scenarios of destruction ‘now regular occurrences’, as he prepares to address Cop31 
 
 
Cop31 live – latest updates  
 
UK politics live – latest updates  




The national security of all countries is at risk from the climate crisis, as “science fiction” scenarios of widespread destruction are already coming true and economic shocks from fossil fuels are now the norm rather than the exception, the UK’s foreign secretary is to warn world leaders gathered in Turkey.
Ed Miliband will tell the Cop31 UN climate summit on Wednesday that security and defence objectives are the new “frontier” of climate action, because the rapid heating of the planet will lead to food shortages, widespread economic disruption, migration and conflict.

“National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action; the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news,” Miliband told the Guardian before his speech to world leaders and governments in Antalya.
“We should be clear that climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face. Food security, threats to infrastructure, and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis],” he said.


View image in fullscreen
Miliband will argue that the world must now face the consequences of failures to cut emissions over the past three decades Photograph: Kenzo Tribouillard/Pool AFP/AP
In a veiled swipe at the Conservatives and Reform UK, which want to scrap efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, he added: “Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.”


Miliband arrived in Turkey on Tuesday evening for the two-day leaders’ summit segment on Wednesday and Thursday of the fortnight-long Cop31 talks, which started on Monday.
Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, is expected to travel on Wednesday for a series of bilateral meetings with fellow world leaders on Thursday.


View image in fullscreen
The Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, watering an olive sapling as the UN chief, António Guterres, and world leaders watch. Photograph: Metin Aktas/Anadolu/Getty Images
Anthony Albanese, the prime minister of Australia, and the Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, will open the leaders’ summit segment on Wednesday. There will also be speeches by the UN secretary general, António Guterres, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil, which hosted last year’s Cop, and the prime minister of Ethiopia, Abiy Ahmed, who will host next year’s meeting.

View image in fullscreen
The remains of a northern gannet, probably a victim of avian influenza, washed up on a beach – H5N1 is now a conservation threat to at least 40 bird species, according to BirdLife International. Photograph: Matthijs Wetterauw/Alamy


Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow?


As the IUCN global conservation body prepares to update its red list of endangered species, scientists explain why calculating the true toll of a pandemic is so hard




It began with the brown skuas. The migratory seabirds had arrived on the sub-Antarctic island of South Georgia in 2023, harbouring a deadly passenger. Within months, the southern elephant seals that had come ashore to breed became sick. Mothers and newborn pups were weak and trembling, with many struggling to breathe. What followed was a horrific mass casualty event, caused by the highly infectious avian influenza (H5N1).
By 2025, more than 53,000 female elephant seals had died on South Georgia. That is especially alarming, scientists say, because the island is home to more than half of the global breeding population.

A highly potent strain of the bird flu virus, which first began circulating in the northern hemisphere in 2021, has now spread to four of the five main southern elephant seal populations. In some South Atlantic colonies, more than 90% of newborn pups have died, alongside about half of all adult females.


View image in fullscreen
A southern elephant seal with a pup at Gold harbour, South Georgia. By 2025, more than 53,000 female elephant seals had died on the island. Photograph: Ashley Cooper/Alamy
“This is a horror show for wildlife,” says Ruth Cromie, coordinator of a UN taskforce on avian influenza and wildlife. “The scale of mortality is absolutely unprecedented.”
In April, the mass deaths prompted the IUCN red list, the global authority responsible for assessing the extinction risks of wildlife, to downgrade the southern elephant seal’s conservation status by two categories, from “least concern” to “vulnerable”.
It was the first time a species has had its extinction risk raised explicitly because of H5N1.


View image in fullscreen
Dead elephant seals on South Georgia in January 2026. Photograph: Jane Younger
The IUCN listing notes that scientists suspect the global southern elephant seal population has declined by nearly a third, and models suggest many populations will take decades to recover. So far, scientists have found few antibodies to the disease among surviving animals.

Developing countries in limbo as rich nations delay new climate finance plans


Many governments are yet to set targets, leaving recipient countries struggling to plan and attract private investment




Developing countries have been left in limbo by the failure of some of the world’s biggest economies to flesh out their plans for new climate finance.
Poor countries are supposed to receive $300bn a year from the governments of industrialised nations by 2035, along with about $1tn from other sources, to help them cope with the effects of extreme weather and shift to a low-carbon future.

But many rich governments have not yet set out their targets and plans for providing climate finance beyond the end of this year or next. This gap is damaging because it means recipient countries cannot plan and makes it harder for them to attract private sector investment to supplement the public sector money.







UN chief urges Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia to turn fossil fuel promises into action

Read more
Analysis by the NRDC and E3G thinktanks seen by the Guardian shows that the developed world is broadly on track to meet the $300bn a year goal – known as the NCQG, or national collective quantitative goal – set at the Cop29 conference two years ago. By 2030 they should be providing about $229bn a year. The multilateral development banks should provide about $185bn of that.
Joe Thwaites, international climate finance director at the National Resources Defence Council, co-wrote the original analysis along with the E3G thinktank and told the Guardian that unless development banks and national governments made sharp cuts in the next round of financing, which is unlikely, then the level of finance needed by 2030 would be almost met.
“Most countries look in quite good shape on climate finance,” he said. “The problem is that they’re not being very public about it.”


If the EU continues its current provision of about $36bn a year (which is likely) then – taking into account the pledges already made by the UK, Canada and some other smaller countries – there would remain a gap of about $7bn to fill.
If a different president is in the White House, the US could make up some of the shortfall, along with Japan and Australia, which have yet to set out climate finance goals, according to Thwaites.
Further analysis by Carbon Brief suggested that if countries failed to implement any new climate finance after their current targets expire, the developing world would face cuts of 70% in bilateral finance (which excludes the development banks) from the rich world. But Thwaites said this was highly unlikely.

articles.jina_text:
Why are Britain’s streets still so polluted? Because the car industry dinosaurs do what they like, and politicians let them

George Monbiot



The transition to electric vehicles should be moving apace, but it is not. And why? Incompetence, expedience and cowardice




This is how it works. An industry puts tremendous effort into resisting change: lobbying governments, mobilising the media, pouring money into junktanks. It argues that a transition would threaten jobs, or damage the national interest, or harm poor people, while what it really fears is the cost of retooling its plants or developing new protocols. Then, when the inevitable cliff edge approaches, it whines that change is coming too soon. For reasons beyond its control, it isn’t ready, so the government must delay its plans.
This is what triggered the Dutch nitrate crisis, and the UK’s repeated “emergency” exemptions from the ban on a devastating class of pesticides. Now the same dynamic is driving the UK’s crisis over the transition to electric vehicles (EVs). The result is that, as the global climate summit, Cop31, begins, it looks as if our gift to the world will be a major, predictable and entirely avoidable increase in the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions.



Car manufacturers could have seen this coming more than 130 years ago, when the first electric automobiles were sold. For at least the past 30 years, as new electromotive technologies have progressed at speed, they plainly represented the future, and internal combustion engines, with their hard efficiency limits and vast impacts on human and planetary life, the past. Since 2010, it’s been obvious that China, which has not only seen the future but seeks to own it, would flatten our manufacturers like hedgehogs if they didn’t speed up. In 2023, the Conservative government gave automakers seven years to get their act together. And now they wring their hands and claim to be unprepared. To which the only reasonable answer is: tough.
But, unfortunately, this doesn’t seem to be the answer the government is giving. Instead, on Wednesday it’s expected to cut the target for zero-emission cars from 80% of new car sales by 2030 to approximately 60%. If so, this will be the latest in a series of concessions that governments have agreed since the Conservatives announced the deadline.
Both Conservative and Labour governments have permitted a series of “flexibilities” (otherwise known as loopholes). These allow companies to sell hybrid petrol-electric cars instead of purely EVs. They can also sell a lower proportion of EVs by 2030 on the promise that they’ll accelerate sales after that date. Now the government is also expected to extend the “flexibilities” to 2034, making a mockery of the promise to accelerate after 2030. One retreat after another.

articles.title: 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted
articles.raw_rss: Forecasters warn that this year's El Niño could be one of the strongest on record, with heavy rain and flooding in Kenya.
articles.raw_meta: Forecasters warn that this year's El Niño could be one of the strongest on record, with heavy rain and flooding in Kenya.
articles.jina_text:
"It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the 6ft [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya.
Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi.
The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water.
Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives.
"Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it."
With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid - especially following warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding.
"I feel like it can kill us. These houses aren't made of stone," says the 62-year-old. "They can fall on us, or the water can drown us."
Kibera - and Kenya more widely - are on the front line of preparations for the potential impact of El Niño.














Forecasters have warned that this year could see one of the strongest on record, bringing extreme weather to many parts of the world.
In southern Kenya, that means the threat of rains even more intense than usual.
Outside Shikoli's house, groups of men and women wearing high-visibility vests are shovelling and raking garbage out of the riverbed and disposing it far from the water.
This programme called Climate Worx, under the office of President William Ruto, is meant to rehabilitate Nairobi's rivers. Such exercises have intensified since August when warnings increased about the possible scale of this year's El Niño.


Rubbish clogging Nairobi's drains and sewers was seen as a major factor in the deadly floods earlier this year
Similar work to unclog drainage systems is ongoing across Nairobi, a sprawling city built on hilly ground crossed by three major rivers.
But the workers have a huge task on their hands.
Blocked drains and inadequate sewage systems were widely blamed for the high number of deaths after the floods earlier in the year, as the excess rainfall had nowhere to escape.










The Nairobi County disaster management chief, Bramwell Simiyu tells the BBC that drainage systems have been "untouched for many years" and that removing the rubbish from them will save lives.
Floods disproportionately affect informal settlements in Nairobi, especially those near rivers, like Kibera and Mathare.

articles.jina_text:
Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist who inspired global climate protests several years ago, said climate change is “threatening everything” and that “everything and everyone we love is at stake.”
In comments reported by AP, she told reporters in Antalya: “We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority, and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she told reporters.
Cop31 is the first UN climate summit Thunberg has attended since the Cop26 conference in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2021, where she dismissed promises made by global leaders as “blah, blah, blah.”
Since then, fossil fuel emissions have continued to rise – though they flatlined this year – adding even more planet-heating gas to a beleaguered atmosphere. While many big polluters have taken steps to clean up their economies, none are doing so fast enough to keep global heating to the 1.5C Paris climate target.

Greenpeace has unveiled a giant limestone boulder carved into the likeness of Sir David Attenborough, which it plans to throw into the North Sea to deter bottom trawling.
Dubbed the “Attenboulder”, the sculpture was revealed aboard the campaign group’s ship Arctic Sunrise on the River Thames on Tuesday.


View image in fullscreen
The “Attenboulder” on the MY Arctic Sunrise. Photograph: Andrew McConnell/Greenpeace
It will join the boulders Greenpeace placed in the Southern North Sea marine protected area earlier this month, in protest at the lack of restrictions on fishing in most of it. The Marine Management Organisation has threatened legal action unless Greenpeace stops placing boulders.
The unveiling comes as Blue Planet III renews attention on ocean protection.
Will McCallum, Greenpeace UK’s co-executive director, said: “Right off our coasts the government still allows industrial fishing vessels to bulldoze the seabed and all of the incredible marine life it holds.
“These are supposed to be safe havens for wildlife – not killing grounds. The government’s inaction makes a mockery of the term ‘marine protected area’ and is an insult to Attenborough’s urgent work over many years.”

More than 700 groups ranging from trade unions to disability advocates have urged diplomats to prioritise a “just transition” for the people who will be hit hardest by a shift to a clean economy.

The Labour-led London authority is behind on its target to replace inefficient gas boilers with heat pumps in council-owned properties

Hounslow Council is behind on 80 per cent of the measures needed to meet its ambitious 2030 net zero target, raising fresh doubts over whether the west London borough can become carbon neutral within four years.






Council documents show a series of flagship climate projects have stalled or fallen behind schedule, despite the authority declaring a climate emergency seven years ago.




The council, currently led by a minority Labour administration, declared a climate emergency in 2019 and adopted a climate action emergency plan five years later.





But one year on from its “refreshed” action plan, 80% of its policies are off track.




Its ambitious net zero target is 20 years ahead of the UK Government, which is aiming for the country to effectively be carbon neutral by 2050. 




There is a right-wing movement attempting to push back against net zero policies, which critics claim could stunt economic growth and lead to higher bills.








That is despite the UN warning recently, ahead of the major global Cop31 environmental conference taking place in Turkey this week, that the world will overshoot the key climate threshold of 1.5C warming above pre-industrial levels, beyond which extreme weather events is likely to become more intense and frequent.




In west London, the net zero pledge at highest risk of not being delivered is Hounslow Council’s aim to decarbonise the council’s entire operational estate. 


Hounslow House 
LDRS / Google Maps




The authority’s target includes replacing inefficient gas boilers with heat pumps, installing solar panels and installing energy efficacy measures.




However, only one of the council’s 37 buildings has been decarbonised, with this section of the project rated “high risk” because “the funding required to deliver decarbonisation of council operations to achieve net zero by 2030 is significant, and not currently identified or available”.




A further 29 assets have been partially decarbonised, and seven have not been decarbonised at all.




Hounslow has also committed to decarbonising 16,000 council-managed social homes by 2030. 




Progress on the move stalled this year, with only 150 homes fully decarbonised, and no further homes decarbonised in 2026.

articles.jina_text:
The world has again convened for Cop, the annual ritual to confront humanity’s greatest-ever threat. Aside from its own lore and acronyms, this conference is starting to feel a little like Groundhog Day.
Representatives from almost all countries, bar the recalcitrant version of the US under Donald Trump, are here in Antalya, Turkey, to face a familiar if worsening challenge. (Even the Taliban are attending.)

The UN, which oversees these talks, has acknowledged the obvious fact that the previously agreed 1.5C global temperature-rise limit is set to be breached in just a few years, with the Earth amassing heat at an accelerating pace.
Wealthy countries, though, are still failing to meet commitments to assist poorer, vulnerable nations to cope with climate impacts. We are still cutting emissions far too slowly. We are still bickering over who should shoulder the most responsibility for this.


So what’s to be gained from Cop31? We’ll go into what to expect over the next two weeks, after this week’s most important reads – and a reminder that, through Cop31, Down to Earth will be coming to you twice a week from Guardian reporters here in Antalya.
Essential reads
 
 
Cop31: what is at stake at the UN climate summit and what can it achieve?  
 
‘A new age of climate extremes’: Earth accumulating heat at accelerating rate  
 
Alien menace or victim of xenophobia? The battle over Britain’s parakeets  
In focus


View image in fullscreen
This year’s summit is an ‘implementation’ Cop. Photograph: Antonio Bat/EPA


Since 1995, Cops have been vital in bringing the world together on the vexed question of the climate crisis, using the unwieldy cudgel of consensus decision-making and peer pressure to help forge the Paris agreement to limit the damage.
In many respects, this has been a success – at one point, the planet was staring down the barrel of a cataclysmic 4C temperature rise this century. That increase is now more in the range of 2.5C, aided by booming growth in clean energy. Such a warping of our climate is still disastrous (just think of the hellish summer many endured merely with the current level of global heating), but Cop has helped steer us away from even worse.
Still, some of the 100,000 delegates gathering here on the Mediterranean coast have been asking what, exactly, can be done here? The terms of the challenge don’t need further debate or agreement, we just have to start following through on our collective promise. Cop31 is another “implementation” Cop – its success hinges on countries going home afterwards and actually implementing things, rather than making more promises in an air-conditioned conference hall.

US and rest of world must follow China’s lead on green energy, says John Kerry


Former US secretary of state says most nations are ‘stumbling along’ while Beijing has ‘hugely accelerated’ 
 
 
Cop31 live – latest updates  




China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.
As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.

Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.


View image in fullscreen
Electric cars imported from China at Southampton docks, UK. Photograph: Filby Photography/Alamy
Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.


Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.

articles.jina_text:
Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.
Carbon dioxide from oil, gas and coal is forecast to flatline for 2026, based on data from the year so far, according to a comprehensive assessment by scientists. Emissions from burning oil alone will drop by 2% as drivers economise on fuel use and flock to electric vehicles instead.



View image in fullscreen
Electric vehicles charge in the parking lot of the Ultium Cells facility in Lordstown, Ohio, in the US Photograph: Quinn Glabicki/Reuters
The findings, presented on Tuesday morning at the Cop31 climate talks hosted by Turkey in Antalya, show both the impact of the Iran war and the global expansion of cheap renewable energy, chiefly solar and wind power.
Talk of a global turnaround would be premature, however, the report’s authors and other analysts said. The report was published in Nature Climate Change. The reduction in emissions from fossil fuels for 2026 will be about 0.4% compared with last year.

Yet this year’s slight fall could be temporary, and was more than offset by increased emissions from deforestation and land use change, following major fires in south-east Asia and further conversions of wild land to agriculture.


Many factors could disrupt the fragile trend of slowing emissions from fossil fuels, including an intensified expansion of coal in India, an easing of oil prices and US president Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for fossil fuels. Much greater investment in renewable energy, and low-carbon technology such as electric vehicles, would still be required to make permanent reductions in annual emissions, the report’s authors said.
Glen Peters, research professor at the Cicero Centre for International Climate Research, said: “A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak, unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles are pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions.”
About 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 will be emitted this year, according to the Global Carbon Budget, an annual assessment by scientists from scores of universities and science institutions around the world, published in the journal Earth System Science Data.



Energy demand continues to increase around the world, as more people gain access to electricity and are pulled out of poverty, but two-thirds of the increase is being met from rising generation from the sun and wind and the uptake of electric vehicles.
On the downside, emissions from deforestation and the conversion of land to agriculture have also ticked upward this year, leading to total carbon emissions rising slightly for the year, from 42.8bn tonnes last year to 43.3bn forecast for 2026.

These findings were presented at the Cop31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey. However, scientists warn the drop could be temporary, as increased emissions from deforestation and land use change offset the gains, and factors such as coal expansion in India and US support for fossil fuels could disrupt the trend.

articles.jina_text:
Dense fog has led to a “high” air pollution alert being issued in London, as forecasters warn of transport delays and difficult travel conditions across much of the country.




Government monitoring recorded the South East and East Midlands as having “high” pollution, with Greater London recorded as “very high”.








The Met Office earlier issued a yellow fog warning for parts of England and Wales, with visibility reduced to less than 100m in some places overnight.




Dense fog has led to a “high” air pollution alert being issued in London, as forecasters warn of difficult travel conditions across much of the country




Forecasters at Imperial College London advised Lord Sadiq Khan of Tooting to trigger the alert “after dense fog and very light winds allowed pollution to build up over the weekend, and linger into Monday morning”, according to the mayor’s office.




It said that smoke from Bonfire Night and Diwali fireworks “is likely to have contributed”.




Londoners have been advised to walk, cycle and use public transport more frequently, drive less and avoid unnecessary burning at home.




Mete Coban, the deputy mayor for environment and energy, said: “Toxic air is responsible for thousands of premature deaths in London each year, which is why the mayor has done everything in his power to tackle it, which includes launching the world’s largest clean air zone.




“It is really important we all do our bit to protect those who are most vulnerable as we continue working to build a safer and greener London for all.”




The alert is the fourth issued in the capital this year, with the last one made in June during a heatwave.












A yellow fog warning is in place until 10am on Tuesday, with the Met Office forecasting a “night of dense fog”.




The affected area stretches from Luton to Manchester, covering parts of central and northern England and Wales.








The Met Office has said slower journey times with delays to public transport are possible, with a chance of delays or cancellation of flights.




The fog is expected to develop across the warning area on Monday evening and will become dense at times overnight – with visibility reduced to less than 100m, according to the forecaster.




It will thin and clear during Tuesday morning, but will give way to cooler and frosty weather later in the week.

Londoners are being warned of high levels of air pollution after days of dense fog and light winds allowed harmful particles to build up across the capital.




Mayor Sadiq Khan has triggered a high air pollution alert for Tuesday following advice from forecasters at Imperial College London, with vulnerable residents particularly urged to take care.








The warning comes as the Met Office issues a separate yellow fog alert for large parts of England and Wales, with visibility expected to fall below 100 metres in some areas overnight.




Forecasters say dense fog and very light winds allowed pollution to accumulate over the weekend and linger into Monday morning, with smoke from Bonfire Night and Diwali fireworks, as well as wood burning, likely to have contributed.




A statement from the Mayor’s office adds: "High levels of particle pollution are forecast for Tuesday after dense fog and very light winds allowed pollution to build up over the weekend and linger into Monday morning.”




It is the fourth high air pollution alert issued in London this year.


Tower Bridge shrouded in fog in London
PA




The Mayor is encouraging Londoners to help reduce pollution by walking, cycling or using public transport where possible, avoiding unnecessary car journeys and refraining from burning wood or garden waste.











Information has also been shared with GPs and emergency departments across the capital to help them support vulnerable patients.




Warnings will be displayed across London's transport network, including Underground services and bus stop countdown signs, while schools and London boroughs will also be notified.







Some London boroughs are covered by the highest levels of pollution, according to air pollution maps provided by the Apple Weather app.




The City of Westminster, Wandsworth, Lambeth, Merton, Ealing, Brent, Tower Hamlets, Greenwich and Bexley are all rated 10, with most of the other boroughs being rated 8 or 6, including Croydon, Richmond upon Thames and Kensington and Chelsea.

articles.jina_text:
Good morning. After another year of unprecedented droughts, floods and wildfires driven by human-caused global heating, 91 heads of government will meet tomorrow in Turkey to discuss the climate crisis. They will do so against a backdrop of global instability and conflict.
But as high-ranking officials and civil society campaigners settle in for a fortnight of speeches, protests and labyrinthine negotiations at the UN’s 31st annual climate conference, Cop31, many are asking what the point is.

Those same governments pledged more than a decade ago in Paris, at Cop21, to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels, but implementation has been sclerotic, and only two months ago a UN report warned temperatures will reach at least 1.8C using even the most optimistic future projections.
I spoke to the Guardian’s environment editor Fiona Harvey in Turkey about what’s on the Cop31 agenda, what success looks like and why Brazil’s re-elected president Lula will be the star of the conference.
Five big stories
 
 
UK | Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after a judge praised his victims’ bravery and accused him of living “unhindered by the rules by which decent people live”.  
 
US | Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.  
 
Russia | US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.  
 
Technology | Palantir lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI technology into GP records, stretching its reach into the NHS in a way doctors fear could undermine trust with patients.  
 
Climate | Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.  
In depth: Why the world is still failing to turn climate promises into action


View image in fullscreen
A Brazilian delegate arrives on the opening day of the Cop31 annual UN climate conference in Antalya. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA

articles.title: The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change
articles.raw_rss: The global campaign to restore the "soggy secret weapon" that can combat against climate change.
articles.raw_meta: The global campaign to restore the "soggy secret weapon" that can combat against climate change.
articles.jina_text:
Most people know rainforests are vital in the fight against climate change, but now scientists say wetlands could be even more important.
Saltmarshes, mangrove swamps and wetlands can absorb carbon "four times faster than trees", according to the charity the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT).
Celebrating 80 years since WWT's first wetland bird reserve was founded at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, the charity's leaders have called for one million hectares of wetlands to be restored across the world.
Sarah Fowler, CEO of WWT, said: "They are mood-boosting, flood-buffering, water-purifying, incredible habitats. But we have lost 85% of the world's wetlands."





Image caption, 

Sir Peter Scott feeds migrating swans and geese at Slimbridge in 1947, with Desmond Hawkins, BBC features producer from Bristol




WWT now runs 10 wetland bird reserves across the UK.
Many people come to enjoy the swans, geese, flamingoes and migrating wildfowl, but do not realise how powerful these habitats can be in soaking up carbon and slowing down climate change.
So how vital are wetlands for birds, and how powerful can they be in the fight against climate change?



'Patron Saint of Conservation'




In November 1946, a naturalist called Peter Scott came to a wild marshy area on the banks of the River Severn, near Slimbridge. He was drawn by the thousands of migrating geese and swans that flew thousands of miles from the Russian Arctic to spend the winter here on the mudflats and marshes.
Captivated, Scott settled in a small cottage and later built a house right on a lake, with a huge window to watch the wildfowl. 
He dug lakes and connecting channels, built hides and even towers to watch the birds without disturbing them.
Over the years, the reserve grew and became home to thousands of ducks, swans , geese as well as the migrating wildfowl.




Image source, WWT Slimbridge
Image caption, 

Sir Peter Scott with the first nine Nēnē geese he hand-reared at Slimbridge in 1952




"He really was a pioneer in conservation," said Chris Moore, a historian of Slimbridge and author of Peter Scott and the Birth of Modern Conservation.
As well as creating a safe haven for endangered species, Scott was a vigorous campaigner for nature. 
He led the fight to stop commercial whaling, presented some of the BBC's first natural history programmes called live from Slimbridge, and helped set up WWF, the World Wildlife Fund.
In 1973 Sir Peter Scott became the first person to be knighted for conservation work.
Moore explained: "Scott was talking about the impact that man was having on the natural world, long before we started talking about climate change and global warming.
"David Attenborough called him the Patron Saint of Conservation, and I think that is more than deserved," Moore added.

Senate advances bill to speed up projects from gas pipelines to clean energy


Key environmental groups come out against bipartisan Baaja bill over fears it could spur datacenters and ICE jails




The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for datacenters and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.
It’s a bill that would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America – everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal. That is why climate advocates are torn over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs act (Baaja).

The Senate voted on Monday to open debate on Baaja in the first of several procedural votes. Senators voted 73-25 on the cloture motion, which did not result in the bill being passed, but pushed it another step forward.



Trump urged all senators to vote for the 417-page bill, which is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats in the Senate, but after last week’s historic “blue wave” elections, some environmental and tribal advocates called on Democratic leadership to pump the brakes.
Earthjustice, the Sierra Club and the ACLU have come out against the bill because it would significantly weaken environmental laws including the National Environmental Policy Act (Nepa) and accelerate the construction of gas pipelines and ICE detention centers.
Indigenous groups held a press conference on Friday calling on senators to vote against Baaja because it would weaken the federal government’s legal obligation to consult tribes on projects that affect them.
“This is such an existential threat to Indian country,” said Mark Macarro, president of the National Congress of American Indians.


View image in fullscreen
Activists protested outside the home of Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer on 6 November, calling out his support for rolling back environmental laws that would increase datacenter projects. Photograph: Michael Nigro/Pacific Press/Shutterstock

Chris Bowen faces a titanic task at Cop31. What will it take for the world to make the climate crisis its top priority?

Adam Morton



Whether the global community can bring itself to name fossil fuels as the cause of the climate emergency will be at the centre of debate in Antalya




Australian politics could have looked markedly different this week if the Albanese government had succeeded in its longstanding bid to host a major UN climate summit in Adelaide.
Tens of thousands of people, including ministers and diplomats representing 200 countries, would have descended on the city of the toxic algal bloom to meet, lobby and negotiate over how to tackle the climate crisis, and wander the halls of a massive green trade fair that runs alongside the formal talks.

For two weeks, it would have been the biggest news story in the country. It would have blocked out the sun. Instead, an estimated 100,000 people are flooding the streets of Antalya, a Turkish resort city on the Mediterranean, for the summit known as Cop31.







High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer’, UN climate chief tells Cop31

Read more
Some senior members of the Albanese cabinet are not sorry they are so far away and lost enthusiasm for hosting the event before the final decision was made. Aside from the climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, the government has shown a diminishing appetite to make the case that fighting global heating is a top priority.
It still has the policies it brought in after the 2022 election – to underwrite large-scale renewable energy, make electric vehicles more available and affordable, and put a limit on industrial pollution – and last year added a generous household battery subsidy scheme. But meeting its emissions reduction targets will require significantly more. So far, those steps are MIA.
Meanwhile, the government continues to approve new coal and gas extraction, mostly for export. Since its election, 38 developments have been given the green light.
It continued a long-term trend. Since 2005 – the year against which Australia measures its emissions reduction targets – annual domestic emissions are estimated to have fallen by 25%. But, according to analysis by Naru Research, emissions from burning Australian fossil fuels after they are exported overseas have roughly doubled. A worker at the Zubair oil and gas field in Iraq. Scientists have confirmed global heating will reach at least 1.8C, beyond the 1.5C goal set at talks in 2015. Photograph: Haidar Mohammed Ali/AFP/Getty


High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer’, UN climate chief tells Cop31


Simon Stiell makes opening address at summit in Turkey, where talks are under way about speeding up shift to electrification




A global fossil fuel price crisis is “spreading inflation like a cancer” around the planet, the UN’s climate chief, Simon Stiell, told the opening plenary of critical UN climate talks in Turkey.
Stiell joined Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia, which is leading the negotiations, in promoting renewable energy and a new electrification goal as an optimistic alternative to a planet still tied to oil, coal and gas.

Inside the tight security of the opening plenary on Monday, delegates from almost 200 countries watched a stirring short film with scenes of fire, flood and storms that proclaimed: “It’s time to reconnect with the planet we have grown apart from.”
Turkey said it expected 100,000 visitors, including national delegations, to attend the two-week talks, including at least 95 heads of state. A global leaders summit is scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday. But the talks are under increased pressure to deliver, after growing dissatisfaction with the snail’s pace of results.


View image in fullscreen
Activists take part in a fossil of the day demonstration on the opening day of the UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya on Monday. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters
The talks are opening as a historic El Niño builds in the tropical Pacific and months after a glacier collapse set off catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet, wiping away villages and killing at least 1,459 people, with thousands more still missing. Climate scientists confirmed this year that global heating would reach at least 1.8C – beyond the 1.5C temperature goal that countries promised to aim for at talks in Paris in 2015.


Last week Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, told the Guardian that although he still had faith in the negotiating process, “the fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast … and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”
And in a statement the UN secretary general, António Guterres, urged leaders to “get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need”.

Full SummaryThe Cop31 climate conference has opened in Antalya, Turkey, with an estimated 100,000 attendees facing logistical challenges despite a sense of optimism. UN climate change executive secretary Simon Stiell emphasized the urgency of transitioning to renewable energy and addressed the climate crisis as a global health emergency.
An estimated 100,000 people have descended on the Turkish city of Antalya for the UN’s flagship climate conference, Cop31, and everybody seems to have a story of a taxi not knowing where the official drop-off location is, a broken down shuttle bus, or a seemingly endless queue in the fierce Mediterranean sun. 
Developing country delegations have reported immense frustration at members being unable to attend opening meetings – and it took this reporter just shy of seven hours from leaving his hotel to finally arrive in the “blue” UN negotiating zone this afternoon.
Regardless of this somewhat shaky start, the message has been clear. In his opening address, UN climate change executive secretary Simon Stiell did not mince his words in highlighting how extreme climate events are hitting communities worldwide – while also calling for an urgent push for renewable solutions that are now typically much cheaper than fossil fuels. 





“Global heating is already costing the Earth: Appalling tragedy has hit the Himalayas, adding to the ever-expanding catalogue hitting communities across every region,” he said. “But the solutions are clear: Global renewables saved around half a trillion dollars last year. And another $265 billion in the first half of this year alone.” 
"The urgency of this moment must drive us forward," Stiell added.
