articles.title: Action on energy costs is my overriding aim, says Fahnbulleh
articles.raw_rss: The energy secretary says reducing bills is key to maintaining public support for climate action.
articles.raw_meta: The energy secretary says reducing bills is key to maintaining public support for climate action.
articles.jina_text:
The energy secretary has stressed that affordability is her "overriding objective", as she said reducing bills would be key to maintaining public support for climate action.
Speaking to BBC Panorama, Miatta Fahnbulleh insisted that the government's drive for cleaner power would help to cut energy bills in the long term.
But she conceded that the push to reduce carbon emissions was currently "under pressure" amid discontent at rising prices in recent years.
It comes as ministers grapple with how to respond to a predicted surge in energy prices in January, expected to mark the biggest rise in bills for four years.







Scientists predict 2026 hottest year on record as climate talks begin





Government's EV targets expected to be reduced this week
Labour has faced extra political pressure over its climate ambitions since coming to power, as Reform UK rose in opinion polls and the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch disowned their previous ambition of reaching net zero by 2050.
Both opposition parties have taken particular aim at public subsidy schemes designed to boost renewable sources of electricity generation, arguing that the drive for cleaner energy has driven up costs for consumers.
UK households currently pay one of the highest rates for electricity in Europe. 














Bills have increased due to subsidies but also because of the high price of gas (a fossil fuel) driven up by international conflicts.

Three reasons why UK electricity prices are so high
Asked during her Panorama interview what her main task was, Fahnbulleh replied: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."
In the interview, which was recorded last week, and aired on Monday night, she argued that Labour's push for greener electricity was "one of our routes to delivering affordability".
"The drive to clean power is about decoupling our dependence on global fossil fuel markets," she added. "Ultimately if we have homegrown renewables, nuclear, that's the way in which we will drive bills in the long term."
However, she conceded that struggles over energy affordability were part of the reason the consensus on climate action was "under pressure".
"People want to blame net zero for that. Now, I don't believe that's the case.
"But I'm very clear that part of the way in which we build and maintain public consent is that we've got to show that this transition, which we have to do on climate grounds, is good for people's pockets."





The UK had a record number of heatwaves this summer and suffered successive damaging wildfires, which the Met Office has said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.
Just last month, whilst hosting the UK's first summit on wildfires, Andy Burnham acknowledged that as a result of climate change "the summer we've just had is likely to be a more regular situation going forward".
But he has also vowed to lead a "cost of living government" and reindustralise the economy.

‘People have blasted fireworks into the fog for days to create a deadly smog full of toxic metals, smoke and other particles.’ 
Meanwhile, Dr Matt Swallow from Asthma + Lung UK cautioned that ‘bonfire smoke, fireworks pollution and chilly air can trigger breathing difficulties.’ He emphasised precautions such as standing away from smoke and following medical advice.

From 1h ago


That’s all for today, thanks for tuning in. Here’s a quick recap of the key events:
 
 
The 31st UN climate summit opened in Antalya, Turkey, co-hosted by Australia, which is leading the formal negotiations.  
 
An agenda was quickly agreed – avoiding a fight that has cropped up in previous years – but tensions over money have already begun to rise.  
 
The World Meteorological Organisation warned that the Earth is heating at an accelerating rate, supercharging weather extremes.  
 
The UN climate chief said this year’s fossil fuel cost chaos is “spreading inflation like a cancer”, as the Turkish hosts push to speed up the electrification of the global economy.  
We’ll be back tomorrow with more coverage as the conference gets under way.

Cop31, this year's UN climate summit, kicks off in Turkey


The EU is almost on track to meet its 2030 climate targets, an official report has found, but efforts to cut pollution fall well short of its 2040 and 2050 targets.
The report, published today by the European Environment Agency (EEA), found EU emissions fell by 1.6% in 2025, though at a slower pace than the year before and not deeply enough to put it on track to meet its goals. If all planned climate policies are put in place, its net emissions should fall by 54% from 1990 levels by the end of the decade, just shy of its legally binding target of 55%.
Europe is among the biggest historical polluters of planet-heating gas, having begun the Industrial Revolution and exported its economic system around the world. In recent decades, though, it has championed some of the most dramatic reductions in pollution. The average European now pollutes a little less carbon than the average Chinese person. Both regions have per-capita emissions well below that of the US, Canada and Australia, though considerably greater than India, Brazil and Indonesia.
The EEA report found EU emission reductions in the next five years must be as high as those achieved over the last two decades to meet its targets. But observers fear many of the easy wins have been exhausted, observers fear, while recent rollbacks of climate policy have dealt a blow to the bloc’s credibility.

Full SummaryUnder the EU's Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive, businesses selling to EU shoppers are prohibited from using terms like 'carbon neutral' or 'climate neutral' if those claims rely on offsets purchased outside a product's direct supply chain. The directive aims to eliminate vague environmental marketing by requiring specific proof and independent certification for green claims.
Few people get to watch their own word being pushed out of use in real time. Fewer still celebrate. "I regret coining the phrase 'carbon neutral'," says Dan Morrell, "so I'm absolutely delighted that my word has been banned, which is an extraordinary feeling. I ended up with it in the Oxford English Dictionary and now to see it finally pass away is fantastic."
Since the end of September, under the EU's Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive, businesses selling to EU shoppers can no longer call a product "carbon neutral", "climate neutral" or "climate compensated" because they have bought offsets outside of the supply chain needed for the product itself. Vague words like "eco-friendly" and "green" are on borrowed time too. For a fashion industry fond of a leafy logo, it is the biggest shake-up of green marketing in years.

After a summer of record-breaking heatwaves, wildfires and school closures, Britain is now facing worsening drought.
Yet as the climate crisis intensifies, the international response is under mounting pressure. Countries have been accused of failing to deliver on promises made at previous UN summits, while several major powers are increasingly turning their backs on the process.
However, energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has told The Independent that Britain’s participation at Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, this week is “in the national interest” – both to protect the country from increasingly extreme weather and to seize opportunities in the green economy.




“This summer, we all felt it. Record heatwaves. Homes lost to wildfires. Schools forced to close in the heat,” she said. “Climate change is no longer a warning about the future, or something happening somewhere else. It is here, in Britain, now.”
Her comments come amid growing questions over whether Cop is delivering on its promises. Donald Trump has pulled the US out of the Paris Agreement and begun the process of withdrawing from the UN climate convention, and several other world leaders are also staying away from this year’s summit.

But with the potential return of El Niño threatening to push global temperatures even higher, the prospect of further extreme weather adds urgency to the negotiations.


Key focuses for the UK at the conference, Ms Fahnbulleh suggested, will include pushing clean power, cutting methane emissions, and protecting forests and oceans. “[We will] build resilience to the extreme weather to come, and unlock the finance to make it happen,” she said. 
Ms Fahnbulleh is leading the UK delegation in Turkey, and is set to attend alongside visits from PM Andy Burnham, foreign secretary Ed Miliband, mayor of London Sadiq Khan, and net zero minister Katie White.

articles.jina_text:
From Western Europe to Indonesia, countries have battled wildfires throughout 2026 following record heat from climate change and El Niño





The world is on course for its hottest year on record as the planet is hit with warming from climate change and El Niño, scientists have told BBC News.
The warning comes as world leaders and negotiators gather in Turkey on Monday for the opening of COP31, the latest UN climate summit.
Berkeley Earth, the independent US research group behind the forecast, said that even with two months of the year left it is 95% confident that 2026 will surpass the previous record set in 2024.
The impact of rising heat has been felt acutely in recent months by countries attending COP, with extensive wildfires across Europe and the sudden glacier collapse in Nepal which killed more than 1,000 people.
"We have had a run of record warm years," said Dr Robert Rohde, of Berkeley Earth. "That is what we expect as global warming progresses… glaciers collapsing, record-breaking heatwaves and droughts."
On Friday, the EU's Copernicus climate service confirmed that October was the hottest on record.
But Rohde warned this was just the start. "There is potential for much larger and much more dramatic changes down the line," he said.
The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.














The UN's World Meteorological Organization (WMO) published its own report on Monday, and although more cautious than Berkeley, it has forecast that 2026 will be among the four warmest years on record.
It said that 2027 will provide no let-up, as an unusually powerful El Niño will continue into next year, pushing temperatures higher.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said it "gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts".


The findings underline the challenge facing negotiators gathering in the seaside Turkish city of Antalya for COP31.
At previous meetings the focus has been on reducing emissions - tackling the cause of climate change. But now an increasing number of nations are facing the reality of having to do that alongside adapting to new weather extremes as the planet warms.
"No single COP is a silver bullet. No single conference can bridge the chasm between the science and reality," Simon Stiell, the UN's climate chief, said as he addressed delegates on the opening morning.
But he added "the urgency of this moment must drive us forward. Global heating is already costing the Earth."










Last month the UK defence secretary warned the public and businesses to think about how they would cope with increasing natural disasters, including stockpiling food.

‘A new age of climate extremes’: Earth accumulating heat at accelerating rate



Increased heat will supercharge extreme weather events, warns UN agency as Cop31 climate summit begins




Heat is accumulating in Earth’s systems at an accelerating rate, the UN’s weather agency has reported as the Cop31 climate change summit begins in Turkey, with 2026 on track to be one of the four warmest years on record.
The imbalance between incoming energy from the sun and energy leaving Earth reached its highest level since monitoring began, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its State of the Global Climate update.

That imbalance and the accumulation of heat will supercharge extreme weather events such as heatwaves, droughts and tropical cyclones.
Around the world, the average surface temperature for January to September 2026 was about 1.47C above the preindustrial average, the agency said. Sea surface temperatures hit monthly records and sea level was the highest since records began. The ocean absorbs 90% of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases and 2026 is on track to be a 10th successive year of record ocean heat.


View image in fullscreen
A centre for people experiencing respiratory difficulties in Palangkaraya, Indonesia. More than 11,000 people have been treated during a months-long wildfire crisis. Photograph: REINA/AFP/Getty Images
“We have entered a new age of climate extremes,” said António Guterres, the UN secretary general. “A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst.”


Diplomats and world leaders are meeting on Monday in the Turkish resort city of Antalya for the 31st conference of the parties (Cop) to the UN framework convention on climate change. In 1992, when the convention was signed, the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide, the primary greenhouse gas, was 356.42 parts per million (ppm). In 2025 it was 426.8 ppm, the WMO said. Overall, since 1750, the onset of the Industrial Revolution, the concentration has increased 53%.







Cop31 must deliver climate progress that people can see is real, host says 

Read more
The WMO reported that ocean heat content estimates indicate Earth’s energy imbalance rose at a rate of 0.3W per sq metre each decade for the period 2001–2025, compared with 0.13W per sq metre between 1960 and 2025.
Accordingly, 2026 is on track to be one of the four warmest years on record globally, making 2023 to 2026 the four warmest years since records began.

The United Nations’ annual climate talks open in Turkey on Monday as Cop31 – with experts suggesting we are already heading for a long-term breach of the crucial limit of global temperatures hitting 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.
As nearly 200 countries gather for the two-week summit in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, governments must deal with an energy crisis fuelled by the war in the Middle East and a growing list of disasters, including deadly floods in Nepal, heatwaves in Europe and wildfires in Indonesia.
These UN talks come at a time when global temperatures already stand at about 1.4C above pre-industrial levels, and 1.5C, the goal set under the 2015 Paris Agreement, is very likely to be breached. The UN Environment Programme’s latest report said last month that it is now about managing the overshoot, to then return below 1.5C.





Overshoot describes a period in which temperatures rise above 1.5C before any return below it. articles.jina_text:
The US will be absent from key UN climate talks that start on Monday, a further sign of Donald Trump’s scornful dismissal of the climate crisis. But Democrats’ crushing win in the US midterm elections has delivered a timely shot of optimism to countries now looking beyond the Trump era of climate obstruction.
For the second year in a row, there will be no official US government presence at the annual climate summit, this year known as Cop31 and held in Antalya, Turkey. While almost every other country in the world sends delegations to the talks, Trump has derided the climate crisis as a “hoax” and “bullshit” and triggered the withdrawal of the US from the entire international climate framework.

“This summit rejects reality by failing to acknowledge that extremist climate policies are destroying countries around the world,” a White House official said, confirming that the administration would not send anyone to Cop31.
The snub is so severe that about 20 members of the US Congress heading to the summit have been denied usual state department assistance, requiring them to turn to philanthropic funding for the trip. “I’m glad we found a way to get there, but it is insane,” said Sean Casten, a Democratic congressman who is attending Cop31. “We have a lot of rebuilding to do. It hinges on Congress to maintain diplomatic continuities at Cop and minimize the damage until adults are back in the White House.”


View image in fullscreen
Sean Casten, a US representative of Illinois, in New York City on 24 September 2025. Photograph: John Lamparski/Getty Images for Concordia Annual Summit
Trump’s active support of fossil fuels, evisceration of pollution limits and throttling of clean energy projects has caused the US to become an outlier among wealthy countries, a recent UN report found. While all the other 20 major economies reduced or slowed their carbon pollution last year, the US was a “major exception” by emitting an extra 133m tons of planet-heating gases from the burning of coal, oil and gas, the report states.


Despite the world rapidly surging past “safe” temperature thresholds because of such pollution, and escalating heatwaves, floods, droughts and other calamities, Trump has remained defiant. “If you don’t get away from this green scam, your country is going to fail,” the US president told other world leaders at the UN last year, adding that the climate crisis was “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world”.
But the Democrats’ stunning success in the midterms last week, wresting control from Trump’s Republicans in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, has buoyed delegates gathering in Antalya. While this will be the last Cop with the US as an official party, after Trump exited the UN framework, the midterms have raised international confidence of a looming return and new, post-Trump chapter.

articles.jina_text:
A beef industry-funded effort to teach teenagers about cattle’s climate impact was quietly scrapped following backlash from some ranchers, who disputed the premise that cows contribute to global heating.
The episode is the latest example of the livestock industry’s decades-long battle to determine what US children learn about cows and the climate.

The American Farm Bureau Foundation for Agriculture (AFBFA) and its Food and Agriculture Center for Science Education produce a free science curriculum used by around 1.2m students across more than 100 school districts nationwide.
Late last year, the foundation announced a new lesson exploring “how cattle produce methane and its role within the broader environmental and biological systems”.







Cryosphere faces permanent damage when world overshoots 1.5C, scientists warn

Read more
Within months it had been removed, following online criticism from ranchers, with Brett Kenzy, prominent South Dakota farmer, telling a trade paper “it’s not fair claiming that cows are harming the environment because they’re not”. Kenzy, who chairs a committee of the Ranchers-Cattlemen Action Legal Fund United Stockgrowers of America (R-CALF USA), called the lesson a “slap in the face”.
“We did take it down,” Rick Henningfeld, the AFBFA education director, told an audience at CattleCon, the beef industry’s annual convention, in February. “We heard the feedback, and we are editing it, and our hope is to get it back up quickly,” according to a recording of the event shared with the Guardian.
It hasn’t yet returned. A new lesson on cattle digestion, published in July, makes no mention of methane or climate.
Since the 1990s, the beef industry has worked to shape what children learn about its products. Today, officials behind the curriculum say it “eliminate[s] negative perceptions” of the industry for “future consumers”.
The curriculum is funded by a mandatory levy on cattle sales called the “beef checkoff”. A foundation spokesperson said the topic “cannot be a 45-minute lesson”. The foundation said it is working on a longer version, reviewing research “related to the biogenic cycle” with help from unnamed researchers and university experts. It said the July lesson was “not a replacement”.
A severed climate connection
Animal agriculture advocates often claim the biogenic cycle – in which atmospheric methane breaks down within about 12 years into carbon dioxide that is then reabsorbed by grass – means cattle methane contributes little additional global heating.
But mainstream climate researchers point out that biogenic methane – which comes from living sources such as organic waste, rice paddies and livestock – is a leading cause of climate crisis, even when emissions aren’t rising.

The 72-year-old retired A&E nurse had solar on the roof of his previous home so had experienced the benefits of cheap electricity firsthand.  
But that setup was funded by the Government and he couldn’t afford a full installation at his new home, a detached bungalow in Gainsborough, Lincolnshire. The bungalow’s roof was also north-facing, meaning the prospect of a traditional solar setup was less attractive.



 
Steel installed plug-in solar panels on his property’s south-facing wall two weeks ago. While the grey weather has generated limited savings so far, he expects to save at least £160 by the end of his first year. 
Panels to be paid off in ‘three to four years’ 
Plug-in solar panels are a cheaper, lightweight version of the green technology, which can be plugged directly into a standard socket to provide instant renewable power.  
They became legal in the UK in August and can be bought from a range of retailers including Argos, Homebase and Amazon. The Government has estimated, based on the output of a 800W solar panel kit, that the technology would save people £70 to £110 a year. 
Steel bought two 920W panels from his energy provider, Octopus Energy, at a cost of £650 including all the hardware needed for installation. 



 
The savings have been modest so far due to the weather. His best day over the past two weeks has seen him generate 3.5 kWh of electricity – worth about 90p based on his current electricity tariff.  
“It’s a bit difficult because of the season, because each day the light gets less, so it produces less,” he explained.  
But when the days get longer, Steel believes it “should subsidise for the whole of the day until it goes dark. So it should be quite a saving in the summer”. 

Steel installed the solar panels on the south-facing wall of his home 
Based on his savings so far, he has calculated it will take three to four years for the upfront cost of the panels to be paid off with savings – meaning he expects to save £160 to £215 per year.  
Rising energy bills were a crucial factor for Steel in the decision to invest.  
“Especially as a pensioner it’s something you feel you have limited control over… it’s a little bit of a safety net,” he said.  
‘Panels are big and heavy’  
One of the benefits of plug-in solar panels is that they are lighter and easier to install. They have been promoted as a solution for flat owners and renters, who in theory should be able to move them from house to house.



 
However, Steel warns the panels are still quite “big and heavy”. While he said he and his wife got them up “quite easily”, he noted that he does have experience working as an electrical engineer.  
Steel got his grandson, an electrician, to put a weatherproof double socket on the outside of his property for the panels to plug into.

articles.jina_text:
The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome ... that people can see is real”, its host has said as scores of world leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries gather in Turkey for the UN climate talks.
The high-stakes meeting begins on Monday, as countries around the world grapple with the strongest El Niño weather system on record, supercharged by fossil fuels, which is set to take hundreds of thousands of lives and cause damage costing trillions of dollars.

Friction is expected between the rich and poor worlds over who pays for the impacts of the climate crisis, and the slow pace of cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Temperatures have broken records this year, surpassing the limit of 1.5C above preindustrial levels aimed for in the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
Adão Soares Barbosa, the chair of the Least Developed Countries, a negotiating group of 44 nations, said: “Keeping 1.5C within reach by minimising the duration and magnitude of the overshoot, delivering accessible and predictable climate finance, strengthening adaptation, and addressing loss and damage [caused to poor countries by extreme weather] are not political choices but matters of survival. The credibility of the Paris agreement will be measured not by promises made, but by commitments fulfilled, and lives protected in vulnerable countries.”


View image in fullscreen
Although the summit is being held in Turkey, the formal negotiations will be presided over by Australia.  Photograph: Sandro Basili/Shutterstock
Unusually, the talks will have dual hosts: they will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya but the formal negotiations will be presided over by Australia, following a compromise reached last year over their competing bids.
Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and president of negotiations for Cop31, told the Guardian in an interview: “We need a tangible outcome focused on implementation [of emissions cuts and finance] that people can see is real. We need progress, it needs to be a step forward on previous Cops.”






How do you broker UN climate talks when your own country is a big coal and gas exporter? Chris Bowen is about to find out

Read more
Australia also wants a “strong, ambitious outcome” to raise the plight of low-lying countries in the Pacific region for whom the climate crisis poses an existential threat. “We need to finally elevate some of the issues so important to our Pacific family,” Bowen said. “[Only] 0.2% of the world’s available climate finance goes to small island developing states for adaptation, for countries whose very existence is at stake.”
But climate advocates and more than 500 scientists in Australia said Australia must stop approving coalmines and gas projects if it wanted to escape the charge of hypocrisy.

US datacenter demand spurs increased fossil fuel pipeline projects as rules are discarded



Trump administration has gutted regulations that protect lives and natural resources as pipeline build-out continues




Datacenters are spurring a boom in fossil fuel pipeline projects at a time when the Trump administration is gutting rules that protect from disasters along the lines, a new review of federal records shows.
The report, compiled by the Environmental Integrity Project, also found pipelines are being built to meet demand for natural gas exports fueled by wars in Ukraine and Iran. Federal records identified almost 200 pipeline projects that are proposed or in the works, and would collectively span 17,000 miles (27,000km).

Not only has the Trump administration targeted laws that protect the environment and human health from pipelines’ risks, it has also pledged not to enforce regulations around them, the report adds.







Datacenters were on the ballot. US voters rejected them

Read more
The findings bring into focus a little-considered environmental threat in artificial intelligence and datacenter proliferation – the US already records about 1.7 pipeline accidents, spills, fires or explosions per day, and these projects would almost certainly lead to more.
The pipelines could help supply the at least 98 gas-fired power plants proposed to serve datacenters, and, if all the lines are completed, they would transport about 40% more natural gas daily than what the system carries today.
“This is the largest boom in a couple decades … and it coincides with all this deregulation,” Alexandra Shaykevich, research manager with the Environmental Integrity Project, said. “That’s concerning because the pipelines do usually operate safely, but they can leak and explode, and so there are big risks for communities across the United States.”


Most of the pipelines would carry natural gas across 42 states, though many of them are concentrated in several fossil fuel-producing regions. About 42 are in or cross Texas, 27 are in Louisiana, and nine each are in Pennsylvania and Illinois.
Advocates say they’re especially worried because of the wide-ranging attacks on foundational environmental protections, from the Clean Water Act to the Endangered Species Act, that until recently have been wielded to stop the riskiest projects, protect from accidents or hold polluters accountable.

articles.raw_meta: What are the relationships and dominant interests in play, as the summit kicks off after a bitter row over its hosting?
articles.jina_text:
Hosting Cop was a key pledge from Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese in 2021, while in opposition, before his successful election campaign. But arcane rules meant the country had to wait its turn to bid and was then embroiled in an angry row with Turkey over the hosting. The final compromise put Australia in charge of the negotiations which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya. The bitter taste left by the row lingers and Australia has seemed to some a rather half-hearted host. The country’s media has been much quieter on Cop than previous host countries, and although Albanese will speak at the opening of the leaders’ segment, he is unlikely to stay long.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, will be in daily charge of the negotiations. As aspects of Australia’s energy supply also fall under his portfolio, he has been in the sometimes uncomfortable position of having to boost fossil fuels while insisting on the need for a clean energy transition.


View image in fullscreen
Chris Bowen in the House of Representatives in Canberra. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP
Yet Australia has a positive story to tell on decarbonisation: while remaining one of the world’s major fossil fuel exporters, the country has also invested heavily in renewables, and solar power has now expanded so much that consumers are sometimes offered free electricity.
Turkey


Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Turkey’s autocratic president, showed little interest in climate and environmental concerns before bidding to host this year’s Cop summit.
In the last five years, Cop has also been held in Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Azerbaijan, all in the same broad region. This has given an outsize role to the Arab group of countries, who are neighbours in the region and have a strong interest in ensuring that fossil fuel interests – including their lobbyists – are well represented.
Australia runs the overall direction of the negotiations, and Turkey’s government, with the environment minister, Murat Kurum, has control of the action agenda, a programme of voluntary initiatives. Erdoğan has used this to push forward a key interest of his wife, Emine Erdoğan, in cutting waste and promoting the circular economy. She has called for an end to “throwaway culture” and for recycling instead of landfill – though Turkey still has sites that leak vast quantities of methane.


View image in fullscreen
Emine Erdoğan has called for an end to ‘throwaway culture’. Photograph: Ahmet Serdar Eser/Anadolu/Getty Images
Fatih Birol, the head of the International Energy Agency and one of the world’s leading energy economists, is understood to be one of the advisers behind this year’s emphasis on electrification, displacing fossil fuels with electricity for heating, transport and industrial uses. This could halve the amount of energy we need, and is the next biggest step, after boosting renewable energy generation, needed for a low-carbon world.

articles.raw_content:
Britain could be plunged into a cold snap by the end of this month (Picture: Getty Images)



An unprecedented record early polar vortex breakdown could leave Britain in a cold snap and even blanketed in snow later this month.

The unusual phenomenon, potentially prompted by the El Niño effect, may see the vortex – a large circulation of strong winds high above the Arctic Circle – weaken and even split, thereby sending colder air further south.

British winters are usually kept relatively mild and wet by a constant straight jet stream over the North Atlantic.

However, a possible breakdown of the stratospheric polar vortex (SPV) threatens to disrupt this pattern.

Met Office forecaster Marco Petagna said: ‘At the moment, we’ve got a warming taking place in the stratosphere. The polar vortex in the stratosphere is starting to weaken.’

Jim Dale, an expert at the private meteorological service British Weather Services, said people needed to be prepared for extreme weather events, so they emerge from them with a ‘smile not a grimace’. 
‘Most people think it is never going to happen to them, but we need to be prepared for whatever Mother Nature throws at us’, he told the Telegraph. 
He added that the prospect of a polar vortex breakdown was ‘debilitating, dangerous and hazardous’. 
If a breakdown were to occur this month it could be record-breaking, smashing the record for the earliest event of its kind. 
The previous record for the earliest date was set on November 28 back in 1969. 
Judah Cohen – a climatologist at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) – told Scientific American magazine: ‘This is a big event because it’s so unprecedented.’ 
A key determining factor in the severity of the breakdown’s impact on the UK climate is where the colder winds hit in Europe. 
Current analysis suggests Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Germany could be among the worst affected countries. 
Some previous SSW events have resulted in acute cold snaps in Britain, while others have greater impacted other countries in the Northern Hemisphere.

View image in fullscreen
Turkey is hosting Cop31 in Antalya, while Australia will lead the formal negotiations under an unusual power-sharing agreement. Photograph: Sandro Basili/Shutterstock



Explainer
Cop31: what is at stake at the UN climate summit and what can it achieve?



Delegates from more than 190 countries are gathering in Turkey for climate talks, but the US will be absent




As the planet faces unprecedented human-caused global heating, heads of government are meeting for the next fortnight for the latest round of climate talks. We ask why it matters and what is likely to be achieved.


What is Cop31?
From 9-20 November, world leaders, ministers and high-ranking officials from more than 190 countries are expected to convene in Antalya in Turkey, for the annual UN climate talks. This year, the summit will be hosted by Turkey, but in an unusual twist the negotiations will be presided over by Australia in a compromise deal struck after the two countries vied for the presidency.







Who’s who at Cop31: key players at the climate talks

Read more
While nearly all of the 196 original signatories of the 2015 Paris climate agreement are expected to be present, one glaring absence will be the US, whose president, Donald Trump, has withdrawn from Paris.

How will co-convening work?
Australia will take charge of the formal negotiations where countries thrash out the details of work programmes such as the “just transition”, climate finance and putting the world on track to stick as closely as possible to the Paris agreement goal of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.


View image in fullscreen
The Paris climate agreement was adopted in 2015, committing countries to pursue efforts to limit global heating to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels. Photograph: François Mori/AP


Turkey will take charge of the “action agenda”, the voluntary agreements that work towards the Paris goals but are not legally binding: programmes on cutting waste and achieving a circular economy, cutting methane, improving food security, and – perhaps most important – the electrification of the global economy.

What are likely to be the key issues?
The Paris goal of 1.5C has been breached, but the UN argues that rapid action to cut greenhouse gas emissions would limit the “overshoot” and allow for a return to lower temperatures by the end of this century. For that to happen, countries need to break dependence on fossil fuels and adopt low-carbon technologies faster. The two roadmaps from Brazil – on the “transition away from fossil fuels” and on halting deforestation – will present ways of doing so.

articles.title: Countryside managers prepare for climate change
articles.raw_rss: North Pennines National Landscape's plan includes restoring peatland and wildfire preparedness.
articles.raw_meta: North Pennines National Landscape's plan includes restoring peatland and wildfire preparedness.
articles.jina_text:
Climate change readiness and helping people access the countryside are among priorities in a five-year plan for a national landscape.
The North Pennines National Landscape Management Plan 2026-31 has been adopted by the Cumberland, Westmorland and Furness, County Durham and Northumberland councils.
Work to ensure the North Pennines was "as prepared as possible for future climate challenges" included restoring peatland to help reduce flooding and equipping farmers with wildfire fighting equipment such as drones.
Chris Woodley-Stewart, director of the North Pennines National Landscape (NPNL), said: "In many ways, its the most ambitious plan that we've ever had, but also the most realistic."
National landscapes were formerly known as areas of outstanding natural beauty, and the North Pennines features heather moors, dales, woods and one of England's highest waterfalls High Force.
NPNL is mainly funded by the government and other charitable organisations.
One of the priorities in its management plan announced last month was adapting to "warmer, wetter winters and hotter, drier summers".




Image source, Getty Images
Image caption, 

The area is home to High Force waterfall




NPNL said uplands were "especially vulnerable to the effects of climate change" through rising temperatures, altered rainfall patterns, and increased frequency of extreme weather events.
Mitigation work like protecting existing woodlands and restoring carbon-rich peat soils would help safeguard upland ecosystems but also support downstream communities by "improving water quality and reducing flooding", it said.
One of the area's largest land managers, Raby Estates, said it worked with NPNL on wildfire prevention measures including managing its farmers' fuel loads and providing firefighting equipment.
Duncan Peake, chief executive at Raby Estates, said drone equipment to help spot fires was a "really significant, additional tool in our wildfire control kit".
As part of the management plan, NPNL said it was would also work with farmers who wanted to get the skills and equipment for farm visits.
Peake said farmers on their estate were already taking groups of mostly young people "who wouldn't normally have an opportunity to come to the countryside" to help them understand how farming works.
Woodley-Stewart said: "You can't make people come to the countryside and invest in the local economy, but you can help to create circumstances in which they feel this landscape is for everybody."
He said the five-year plan would guide the policy of the local authorities but would not be compulsory.
"There's no stick here, it's all carrot," Woodley-Stewart said, adding: "Everyone has a role to play in its implementation."

articles.jina_text:
Banana producers in Latin America are calling for better pay to help cope with the impact of the climate crisis, as they face big drops in production resulting from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event.
High winds in parts of Colombia, one of the biggest suppliers to the UK market where droughts are predicted in some regions this year, and heavy rainfall in Peru and Ecuador are already affecting production, according to the Fairtrade Foundation ethical trade body. In the Dominican Republic, farmers are expected to face drought conditions, with forecasts of drier and warmer than usual conditions.

Fairtrade research suggests that during the previous El Niño cycle, productivity across its farmers and workers dropped by 13% in the Dominican Republic, 22% in Ecuador, and 6% in Peru compared with the year before. The El Niño event in 1983 – one of the strongest ever recorded – affected 15% of total planted banana area in Ecuador, with a reduction in exports of 36%.


Dr Carley-Jane Stanton, a climate and environment lead at Fairtrade, says this El Niño is expected to lead to more extreme weather, including heavy rainfall and strong winds and “we expect the impacts for producers to be more severe” than in the 23-24 cycle.
Evidence is mounting to fuel those fears. Exports from the Colombian Caribbean region fell 32% to $122m (£91m) between July and September this year, according to the Association of Banana Growers of Magdalena and La Guajira, as reported by the trade publication Fruitnet.
It said that in September alone, shipments were down 42% year on year, with earnings close to halving to $40m from $70m.
“Given the risks threatening the continuity of banana production, we are calling on international markets to foster commercial conditions that recognise actual production costs and contribute to the sector’s sustainability,” the association said.
It said that climate-related productivity losses and a decline in earnings from exports made worse by currency issues was “undermining the economic sustainability of the industry”.
Ever Antonio Flores Muños, a worker at the Agrosiete banana producer in Colombia, told Fairtrade: “Over the past 10 years the climate has changed a lot. It’s been getting much hotter … it’s really intense. Some places have had losses due to the climate, flooding, strong winds. It’s going to affect all of us – our workers, colleagues – everything will be at great risk, and our wages will decrease.”


Fairtrade is calling for legislation in the UK to tackle unfair trading practices, such as low or late payments to farmers and contracts which push risk down the supply chain, so that producers can invest more into improving their crops’ resilience to severe weather and more likelihood of pests and diseases. Worker health is also expected to be affected by more extreme weather.

Environmentalists criticise choice of Earthshot prize venue owned by fossil fuel firm



Mumbai facility is part of Reliance Industries, owner of world’s biggest oil refinery and funder of controversial mega-zoo




The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo.
A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize, which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.

The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild.
Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.
Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.
This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.
The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.
Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.

National Trust votes to seek banking partner more in tune with its environmental policies



Charity’s AGM decides overwhelmingly to begin tendering process amid criticism of Barclays’ fossil fuel investments




The National Trust has voted overwhelmingly to seek a new banking partner in a significant victory for members who have long argued that its relationship with Barclays was at odds with its commitment to protecting the natural world.
The resolution, passed at the charity’s annual general meeting on Saturday with the backing of its board of trustees, instructs the organisation to begin a competitive tendering process for its banking arrangements.

That process will, for the first time, centre on the condition that the new bank demonstrates a positive commitment to protecting biodiversity and reducing the human-induced climate crisis.
Campaigners said the result, 53,256 votes for and 4,094 against, sent a message that charities should apply the same environmental standards to their financial relationships as they do to their investments and suppliers.


Others questioned the significance of the success, with insiders suggesting that the tendering process will not take place for at least a year.
Despite supporting the vote the National Trust sounded a qualifying note, with Sandy Nairne, deputy chair of the board of trustees, warning: “The outcome of the ballot provides the board with an important indication of members’ views, but it is not binding on the trustees.
“The trustees will carefully consider the result alongside the discussion we have heard today as part of their future decision making,” he added.
“This result highlights a profound shift in NGO accountability,” said Drew James, a proposer of the resolution and a member of Christian Climate Action.
“Civil society looks to charities, universities and faith groups to sever ties with financial institutions failing to match their ethical standards.”
The move follows years of pressure from members concerned about Barclays’ financing of the fossil fuel industry. The bank has been criticised for its support for oil and gas expansion, including fracking and methane gas infrastructure, while the National Trust has repeatedly identified the climate emergency and the decline of nature as the greatest threats to the landscapes, wildlife and historic properties in its care.

Delhi’s air quality fell into the "very poor" category this week, days before the Hindu festival of Diwali was expected to make it worse.
The Central Pollution Control Board classes readings of 301 to 400 as "very poor" and beyond 400 as "severe". 
The deterioration in air quality came after the Indian capital saw the lowest average AQI for October in eight years, at 166, and north-westerly winds carrying smoke from crop burning in neighbouring states returned after a storm.

articles.jina_text:
A wildfire at Lacanau in south-west France in July. Scientists say human-caused climate change has increased the risk of wildfires. Photograph: Maximilien Lamy/AFP/Getty Images



Its key temperature goal has been missed but experts say the agreement is still proving a vital moral compass for progress






 
 
It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.

Brazil was insisting, instead, that these plans – the bedrock of the Paris agreement – were the business of national governments and not up for negotiation. “In that case, it will be a very short Cop,” one seasoned global south negotiator told the Guardian shortly before, reflecting a widespread unease. “There is nothing to negotiate.”
“They have decided that there is no appetite for negotiation, with the US out of Paris,” said another developing country diplomat. “Countries won’t engage.”
The summit ended with a deal, although few loved it. But, as the faultlines from the Brazilian decision deepen going into this year’s summit, it is clear that the Paris agreement, and climate action around the world, has reached an impasse.


View image in fullscreen
André Corrêa do Lago, Cop30 president, sits as Simon Stiell, UN climate chief, left, speaks with other officials at Cop30 in Belém. The summit in Brazil ended with a deal that few loved. Photograph: André Penner/AP
And it is not just Cop insiders who are worried. For many outside the vast white air-conditioned conference halls, the question, as this year’s summit begins, will be: what is the point?
Those same governments have pledged year after year since the Paris agreement was signed in 2015 – and entered into force a year later – to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Yet temperatures for two years have exceeded that threshold, and the UN revealed a few weeks ago that its most optimistic estimate was now for about 1.7 to 1.8C of heating.
There could be no clearer evidence that the Paris agreement, on the face of it, has failed. It is impossible not to wonder whether the Cop process itself is just not fit for purpose.
The charge sheet against Paris is long, with the central issue being the failure to achieve its goal. Beyond that immediate failure, the negotiation processes are endlessly convoluted and cause their own problems. It took more than five years just to negotiate the Paris “rulebook” under which the treaty is interpreted and put into effect.
The convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given bad actors free rein. Donald Trump’s allies – in Saudi Arabia, Russia, Venezuela and some other petrostates – frequently veto measures and obstruct progress.

articles.jina_text:
But after torrential rainstorms linked to the super El Niño season, at least one famous rock formation in north-west New Mexico has been found in pieces.

And as local communities in the Four Corners region struggle with the aftermath of flooding, washed-out roads and damaged homes, more damage to the region’s natural wonders may still be discovered.
Kialo Winters was leading a tour of the Valley of Dreams trail in New Mexico, near the Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah Wilderness, on 30 October when he discovered that one of the area’s most famous spires, or “hoodoos”, had been destroyed.
“We turned the corner, and my heart just dropped,” he said. “The highlight feature that everyone wants to see is the Alien Throne.”



The majestic formation, which is featured prominently on a local tourism website, had broken into pieces. Winters said he immediately assumed that the heavy rains and the super El Niño season were to blame.
A week before, rainstorms and flooding had hit north-west New Mexico hard, forcing evacuations and hundreds of water rescues of stranded residents. In Farmington, the nearest town to the Valley of Dreams area, some families spent the night on rooftops watching the river flood their homes before they were rescued, officials said.


View image in fullscreen
A rock formation in north-west New Mexico. Photograph: Kialo Winters / Navajo Tours USA.


Winters has been guiding visitors to the region for 13 years as part of Navajo Tours USA, a company he founded. The rock spires, which are on Navajo Nation land, are beloved by visitors and photographers, but they also have a deeper significance to the region’s Indigenous residents, he said.
“They are traditional waypoints in our Indigenous history that have guided our people across the land for many generations,” Winters said.
And it was not just the Alien Throne that had tumbled down, Winters said. Another nearby formation, the King of Wings, what Winters called “the unicorn of hoodoos”, has also been damaged in recent weeks. Multiple user posts on AllTrails, a hiking website, suggested the formation had broken sometime before 9 October, before intense rains hit the region.
“Those are heavy losses for us,” Winters said. But, he added: “The land is alive, and we understand it changes. The same erosion that made them also brings them down, that is what our elders tell us.”
Winters called for visitors to the damaged spires to “let that site rest,” and not to climb what’s left of the formations, or take stones home for relics. “It’s illegal to do that,” he said, adding: “It’s disrespectful to the community as a whole.”
While his assumption is that the Alien Throne broke because of “natural causes”, Winters said, the Navajo Nation and the Bureau of Land Management are expected to examine the site and confirm the cause.

articles.title: How climate change worsens heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and floods
articles.raw_rss: Rising global temperatures mean extreme weather events are becoming more common and more intense.
articles.raw_meta: Rising global temperatures mean extreme weather events are becoming more common and more intense.
articles.jina_text:
Many extreme weather events are becoming more common and more intense around the world, fuelled by human activities such as the burning of fossil fuels.
Here are four ways that rising temperatures are affecting weather extremes.
1. Hotter, longer heatwaves
Even a small increase in average temperatures makes a big difference to heat extremes.
As the range of daily temperatures shifts to warmer levels, hotter days become more likely and more intense.


Scientists use computer models to simulate how individual extreme weather events unfold in two scenarios:

today's world with about 1.4C of human-caused warming
a hypothetical world without human influence on the climate














That way, they can estimate how much a particular heatwave, storm or drought was affected by climate change.
The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.
Five widespread heatwaves affected the country, resulting in 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F).
Head of Climate Attribution at the Met Office, Dr Mark McCarthy, described summer 2026 as "remarkable" and warned that extreme heat events would only become more common as the world warms.







A really simple guide to climate change





What is net zero and is the UK on track to achieve it?
Climate change has also intensified multiple heatwaves across the world this year, according to scientists at the World Weather Attribution group (WWA).
Examples include Australia's worst heatwave in six years in January, the 45C that India experienced in April and Europe's deadly June temperatures.
Heatwaves can happen as a result of heat domes, which are created when an area of high pressure stays over the same area for days or weeks, trapping hot air underneath.







Higher temperatures in the Arctic - which has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average - may be affecting the fast band of winds high in the atmosphere known as the jet stream.
One theory suggests that this is making heat domes more likely, although this is not clear cut.
2. More extreme rain
For every 1C rise in air temperature, the atmosphere can hold about 7% more moisture.
With more moisture available, rainfall can become heavier.


UK winters were 13% wetter in the decade from 2016 to 2025 than between 1961 and 1990, the Met Office says.










However, the large annual variation in rainfall makes it difficult to draw conclusions from a single decade, its scientists warn.
Globally, heavy rainfall events have become more frequent and intense over most land regions due to human activity, according to the UN's climate body, the IPCC.
For example, in October 2025, Hurricane Melissa became one of the strongest hurricanes to ever hit the Caribbean.
WWA researchers found that climate change increased extreme rainfall associated with the storm by 16%.
3. Longer droughts

articles.title: A really simple guide to climate change
articles.raw_rss: Human activities are causing the world to heat up, posing serious threats to people and nature.
articles.raw_meta: Human activities are causing the world to heat up, posing serious threats to people and nature.
articles.jina_text:
Things are likely to worsen in the coming decades, but scientists argue urgent action can still limit the worst effects of climate change.
What is climate change?
Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions.
The world has been rapidly warming for around a century, causing weather patterns to change.
Since the 1980s, each decade has been warmer than the previous one, the Met Office says.
2024 was Earth's hottest year on record, with climate change mainly responsible for the high temperatures.
It was also the first calendar year to surpass 1.5C of warming compared to "pre-industrial" levels of the late 1800s, according to the Copernicus climate service.














Temperatures remained high in 2025, despite a slight cooling from a natural weather pattern called La Niña.
The opposite El Niño pattern, combined with climate change, makes it likely that 2026 will also rank among the hottest years ever recorded.


How are humans causing climate change?
The climate has changed naturally throughout the Earth's history.
But natural causes cannot explain the particularly rapid warming seen over the last century, according to the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
This has been without doubt caused by human activities, especially the widespread use of fossil fuels - coal, oil and gas - in homes, factories and transport systems.
When fossil fuels burn, they release greenhouse gases - mostly carbon dioxide (CO2). This CO2 acts like a blanket, trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface. This causes the planet to heat up.










Since the start of the Industrial Revolution - when humans began burning large amounts of fossil fuels - the level of CO2 in the atmosphere has risen by more than 50%.
The CO2 released from burning fossil fuels has a distinctive chemical fingerprint. This matches the type of CO2 increasingly found in the atmosphere.


What effects of climate change have already been seen?
Climate change has already had a huge effect, including:

more frequent and intense extreme weather, such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall
rapid melting of glaciers and ice sheets, contributing to sea-level rises
the shrinking of Arctic sea-ice

articles.title: What is the Paris Agreement and why does 1.5C matter?
articles.raw_rss: The 2015 pact is at the heart of the international commitment to tackle rising global temperatures.

articles.jina_text:
Nepal became the first country approved to receive money from a fund for damages linked to climate change after flash floods in August 2026





In Paris in 2015, almost 200 countries signed a landmark agreement designed to limit global warming to 1.5C and avoid its worst impacts.
But despite some progress in areas like renewable energy, the world has continued to warm at a rapid pace.
A recent UN report said the target was likely to be breached in the next few years and that "urgent and stringent" action would be needed to return the world to 1.5C.
What is the Paris climate agreement?
The Paris Agreement is at the heart of the international commitment to tackle rising global temperatures.
It came into force on 4 November 2016 and saw almost all the nations of the world agree to cut the greenhouse gas emissions which cause global warming.
However, the United States - the world's second biggest greenhouse gas emitter - withdrew from the deal in January 2026 under President Donald Trump.
The US also withdrew during Trump's first presidency, but it rejoined in 2021 under his successor President Joe Biden. 














The only other UN member states outside the Paris agreement are Iran, Libya and Yemen.
What does the Paris Agreement say?
The Paris Agreement lists a series of commitments:

to "pursue efforts" to limit global temperature rises to 1.5C, and to keep them "well below" 2.0C above those recorded in pre-industrial times, generally considered to mean the late 19th Century

to achieve a balance - known as net zero - between the greenhouse gases that humans put into the atmosphere and the gases that they actively remove, in the second half of this century

each country to set its own emission-reduction targets, reviewed every five years to raise ambitions 

richer countries to help poorer nations by providing funding, known as climate finance, to adapt to climate change and switch to renewable energy
The 1.5C target is generally accepted to refer to a 20-year average rather than a single year.





So, while 2024 was more than 1.5C warmer than pre-industrial times, it did not mean the Paris Agreement threshold has been breached


Why does keeping global warming to 1.5C matter?
Every 0.1C of warming brings with it greater risks for the planet, such as longer heatwaves, more intense storms and wildfires, according to climate scientists.
But a very large body of scientific evidence shows that warming of 2C or more would bring far greater impacts, on top of those felt at 1.5C, UN scientists say. 
These include:

more people being exposed to extreme heat
higher sea levels as glaciers and ice sheets melt
increased risks to food security in some regions due to more extreme weather
greater chances of some climate-sensitive diseases spreading, such as dengue
more species being threatened with extinction
the loss of virtually all coral reefs
Some changes could become irreversible if so-called "tipping points" are crossed.

articles.title: What is net zero and is the UK on track to achieve it?
articles.raw_rss: Reaching net zero carbon emissions worldwide is essential to limit global warming, UN scientists say.

articles.jina_text:
Achieving "net zero" is the world's key strategy to fight climate change, which is already having serious consequences for people and nature around the globe.
But the political consensus around the UK's net zero policies has collapsed, with the Conservative and Reform parties now branding them too difficult and expensive.
What does 'net zero' mean?
Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.
Effectively this means no longer adding to the total amount of these gases in the atmosphere to limit climate change.
Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane. Their levels in the atmosphere are increasing rapidly due to human activities, including burning fossil fuels, chopping down forests and farming.
In practice, reducing these emissions means switching from coal, oil and gas to cleaner energy sources like wind and solar power.
It also involves adopting green technologies like electric vehicles and heat pumps to replace petrol or diesel cars and gas boilers.














But not all emissions can be eliminated.
So remaining emissions must be matched by things like planting trees, restoring peatlands or using machines to remove CO2 from the air.
But there are limits to these "carbon removal" techniques in scale and cost. That is why most of the focus is on drastically reducing emissions in the first place.
Why are net zero targets needed?
The world is warming because of humanity's greenhouse gas emissions, which increase global temperatures by trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface.
This is bringing more heatwaves and extreme weather as well as melting ice sheets and raising sea levels.
In 2026, the UK experienced its hottest summer on record, which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.
Aiming to avoid the worst of these impacts, nearly 200 countries signed the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement. A target was set to reach net zero globally in the second half of the century.





Around 140 countries have their own net zero targets, covering roughly three-quarters of global emissions and 80% of the world's population.
It's widely accepted that richer nations will need to get to net zero before poorer ones, which often have fewer resources to switch to cleaner technologies and have contributed less to climate change historically.

The UK's greenhouse gas emissions have fallen sharply: in 2025 they were 54% lower than in 1990, according to provisional data. 
This figure only includes emissions generated within the UK and not from products manufactured abroad and imported.

For two years, Americans have witnessed a largely unchecked assault on the foundations of US democracy. Authoritarian leadership has enriched itself through corruption, spread lies and launched relentless attacks on press freedom, voting rights, due process and many fundamental civil rights.
Last night, America’s embattled democracy came roaring back to life: from Texas to Ohio to South Carolina, Americans surged to the polls to fight for a different path forward. The process worked, the people spoke, the candidates – and the president – accepted the results. Today, we’re on the cusp of a new chapter for America, where the people have claimed their right to hold power to account, and millions are looking at politics with a new and unfamiliar feeling of hope. 
The past two years have delivered a chilling lesson in just how fragile our fundamental freedoms are, when precious few powerful institutions are willing to stand up for the truth and defend our basic rights and freedoms. Major law firms and universities capitulated to a bullying president’s threats and intimidation. Some corporate news outlets bowed to his pressure, too.
In the face of these attacks, the independent press stood out as one of the only forces for accountability, dedicated to uncovering the truth – and making sure the public understood what was at stake in this election.
At its best, a truly free press can speak directly to the public, shedding light on hidden schemes and revealing the whole picture of our flawed world. Yet these are challenging times for press freedom: Trump’s crackdown on the press shows no signs of letting up; consolidated ownership means fewer options and less diversity of perspective; and the advent of AI has threatened the entire business model of journalism, resulting in extreme staff layoffs that have gutted newsrooms.
We will need a free press in 2027 as much as we relied on one in 2025 and 2026. The Guardian is fortunate to have no billionaire owner, no corporate bosses who put profit over mission. We’re accountable to the facts and to our readers. And the Guardian is fortunate to have our readers who are willing to support – and commit month after month – to help sustain our independence.
 From reporting on the ground to fending off legal risks to keeping our reporters safe, journalism is incredibly expensive to do well. To help fund our work in 2027, we are looking to raise $2,000,000 by the end of the year. If you can contribute any amount, please do so. If you can contribute monthly, even better – I need to know we have the resources to report on the final throes of Trump’s presidency in what may be a tumultuous year ahead.


Betsy Reed

The UK’s electric vehicle charging network is vulnerable to cyber attacks from hostile states such as Russia and China that could wreak havoc on roads, The i Paper can reveal.  



Hackers could target Britain’s rapidly growing public network of 125,000 charging points, for which there are no specific cyber security measures.



Home EV chargers – there are around 1.4 million in the UK – must already comply with security requirements set out in legislation, but still have vulnerabilities that hackers could exploit, experts say.  





An attack could take out charging points, leaving motorists unable to power their cars. If several chargers were affected, drivers would be forced to search for alternatives, causing disruption on the roads and at forecourts.  



Recent research by The Hong Kong Polytechnic University also discovered that an attacker need only manipulate EV charging navigation systems to redirect large numbers of vehicles to the same charging station.  



The stark admission that the public network of charging points has no uniform security measures was set out in documents published by the Department for Transport.

View image in fullscreen
Firefighters from Marseille battle a blaze near Bordeaux in July. Devastating wildfires this summer have elevated concerns about the climate crisis in France. Photograph: Emma Da Silva/AP


Most Europeans want action to tackle climate crisis but not at any cost, poll shows



YouGov survey finds support for tree planting and emissions taxes but opposition to air travel and fuel levies 
 
 
Europe live – latest updates  




Europeans believe human-made climate change is real, a survey has shown, with most feeling action must be taken soon – as long as they do not have to sacrifice too much to achieve it.
The YouGov poll of six European countries showed between 69% (Germany) and 80% (France) of respondents believed the climate was changing, with few (1%-4%) denying it and 14-20% believing it was changing, but not as a result of human activity.

Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent and scientists say human-driven climate breakdown through the burning of fossil fuels is increasing the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and destructive storms.
Days before the Cop31 climate conference in Turkey, the polling showed vast majorities (79-89%) in Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK thought countries would combat the crisis more effectively by working internationally.


Those in the EU were more likely to say that climate action decisions should be made at EU rather than national level, a feeling shared by 50-54% of respondents in France, Italy and Germany as well as 61% in Denmark and 64% in Spain.
Majorities of between 65% and 83% in each country surveyed said they were worried about the climate crisis, including 23%-42% who were “very worried”. YouGov noted an uptick in concern during this summer’s heatwaves.
In April, 74% of respondents in France said they were worried about the climate crisis but that figure was up to 83% by mid-August and still at that level last month.
The number of French people who were “very worried” about climate change also rose, from 28% in April to a record high of 42% in August, a level it held last month. Concern in other countries spiked in August but has since dipped.
In Germany, for example, the number very concerned rose from 27% in April to 40% in August but has now fallen back to 31%. Concern remained relatively stable in Denmark, at 66%-69% “worried” and 20%-23% “very worried”.


Across the six countries surveyed, respondents mostly (45%-63%) thought it was not too late to avert the worst impacts of the climate crisis but that it would require a drastic change in approach. Only 11%-24% believed it was already too late.

articles.title: El Niño in Spain to drive up food prices in Britain's supermarkets, warns Bank of England
articles.raw_rss: Cost of food could go up in UK due to El Niño from early next year
articles.raw_meta: Cost of food could go up in UK due to El Niño from early next year
articles.jina_text:
Extreme weather from El Niño hitting countries such as Spain is threatening to push up food prices in Britain, the Bank of England is warning.




The cost of fruit and vegetables is likely to increase first, says the bank which raised interest rates on Thursday from 3.75% to 4%.








El Niño-linked price rises could start to appear in supermarkets, convenience stores, other food outlets and restaurants from early next year.


‘Unprecedented’ El Nino event bringing storms and rain to the UK
PA Wire




The increases could last for many months, the Bank of England (BoE) believes.




Combined with the more modest impact of recent heatwaves which hit the UK and other countries, El Niño could push up the cost of food by two percentage points, it added.




Millions of households in London and across the UK are already struggling with the cost of living and some could see their mortgage bill rise by £600-a-year after the latest interest rate rise by the bank’s Monetary Policy Committee.




Laying out the economic background for the interest rate increase, which aims to control inflation, the bank published its Monetary Policy Report which detailed a range of factors, including weather.












“The current El Niño event is expected to place upward pressure on UK food price inflation,” it said, explaining how extreme weather can hit crop yields in some regions while increasing them elsewhere.




“Overall, the current El Niño is expected to place upward pressure on global agricultural commodity prices and, in turn, UK food prices,” it added. 








“Around a quarter of UK food imports, equivalent to around 10% of total food supply, comes from El Niño-exposed regions.” 




Spain is Britain’s leading provider of fresh produce, particularly out-of-season fruit and vegetables, with large volumes also coming from The Netherlands, France and Germany.

Londoners could also face freezing temperatures this month, as El Niño continues to strengthen across the Pacific to what some scientists are calling “unprecedented levels”.




Forecasters have warned that the global phenomenon could disrupt the polar vortex – a vast ring of freezing winds high above the Arctic that normally keeps the coldest air contained around the North Pole.


Map of the Pacific Ocean and El Nino threat
aapsky - stock.adobe.com




The bank’s indepth analysis also stressed that El Niño could add to pressures in global energy markets by reducing biofuel production, constraining hydroelectric and nuclear power generation, and increasing demand for cooling and energy-intensive irrigation. 












Lower water levels in inland waterways could also disrupt transport networks.

A family of beavers has been released into waters surrounding Loch Ness, marking the species' return half a millennium after they were last spotted there.The animals were released on Wednesday at a lochan within Trees for Life's Dundreggan rewilding estate, a 10,000-acre site in Glenmoriston, after NatureScot licensed their relocation from elsewhere in Scotland.The release marks the first step of the Ness Beaver Project, a joint initiative by Trees for Life and Beaver Trust that both organisations have described as a "major milestone for nature recovery in Britain".Under the scheme, a minimum of 15 beaver family groups will be brought to the Loch Ness catchment area over the coming three years, with the aim of establishing a thriving population across the Highlands.

articles.title: Over 1,000 tonnes of sewage seen at landfill site
articles.raw_rss: The Environment Agency says it has issued the operator with a series of actions after an inspection.
articles.raw_meta: The Environment Agency says it has issued the operator with a series of actions after an inspection.
articles.jina_text:
More than 1,000 tonnes of "sewage sludge" have been seen at a landfill site near Doncaster, according to an MP for the town.
Lee Pitcher said in a Facebook post he had been told the waste was being stored in "an uncovered stockpile" at the site in Finningley.
The Labour MP said he had been in contact with the Environment Agency (EA), which confirmed on Thursday that it had "set out a series of actions" for the site's operator following an inspection.
The landfill, located in a former quarry, is operated by Tetron Finningley Ltd, which has not previously responded when contacted for comment by the BBC.
Pitcher, who is the MP for Doncaster East and the Isle of Axholme, said EA officers visited the landfill on 9 October and, after he "chased" them for their findings, they responded on Tuesday.
He said the EA had told him that during the visit "approximately 1,000 tonnes of sewage sludge were observed being stored externally in an uncovered stockpile" and had "identified concerns regarding whether site activities were being undertaken in accordance with the operating techniques and management arrangements described within the approved documents".
Pitcher said the EA had given the landfill operator until 10 November to resolve the issue.
The MP said he had subsequently contacted the EA again about "potential asbestos disposal at the site, along with the air quality and environmental ramifications this could bring".





Image caption, 

A nearby motocross track closed after riders complained of headaches and dizziness they blamed on the smell coming from the site




Last month, Ed Bradley, a director of the neighbouring Doncaster Moto Parc, said he had been forced to close the venue after people attending the motocross track were suffering from "headaches, nausea and generally feeling unwell" from the smells.
He said he was concerned that the business may no longer be viable if it continues to remain closed.
In a statement on Facebook, he said: "For months, we have raised concerns about the terrible odours coming from the neighbouring site, the effects on our staff and customers, and our inability to operate safely.
"Despite those reports, the situation has continued.
"Unfortunately, while the authorities have been investigating, the financial consequences for Doncaster Moto Parc have been devastating.
"We are now facing the very real possibility of losing the business altogether."
An Environment Agency spokesperson said: "We expect site operators to manage odour effectively and have identified issues around odour management at this site.
"Following an inspection, we have set out a series of actions that we expect the operator to comply with and will not hesitate to take further enforcement action should that be required."
