Climate-forward Democrats swept into power on Tuesday night as a blue tsunami flipped the Senate, House and several governor’s races. Voters were laser-focused on affordability, and experts said Democrats succeeded in linking cost-of-living concerns with rising energy prices, datacenters and, to some extent, the climate crisis. They may have even created a path for a “new climate politics”.
The results delivered a sharp rebuke of Donald Trump, who started a war with Iran that raised gas pump prices across the country and exposed the fragility of fossil fuels, all while the US oil industry earned $130bn in profits since the war began. Household energy costs soared, driven by various factors including constraints on renewables, climate disasters and a datacenter boom.




But how to articulate this before the election was a matter of debate among Democrats known for “climate forward” views: should they talk about the worsening climate crisis directly or keep messaging tight on affordability? Some senior figures including Gavin Newsom warned about “climate hushing”.






A progressive understanding of Christianity won in the US elections

Successful candidates “made connections between the cost of living crisis and the climate crisis, and how the same bad actors – such as utilities, oil companies, corporate landlords, and data center developers – are driving both”, said the analysis, by the thinktank Climate and Community Institute (CCI).
It found the candidates with the “strongest alignment with green economic populism won 39 of 56 (70 percent) of federal races for House and Senate in which they ran, including 6 of 7 in the Senate and 33 of 49 (67 percent) in the House”. The results show that “voters want leaders who will make life affordable and stand up for working people against elites, and climate is a critical part of that equation,” said Johanna Bozuwa, the CCI’s executive director.

Datacenters became a key focus of voters’ ire, he added: “There’s no question it was the biggest crossover issue to get Republicans, Democrats and independents going in the same direction.”

articles.jina_text:
First Minister John Swinney says he does not support the UK government's plans to ban any new exploration for oil and gas in the North Sea.
The SNP leader told MSPs fossil fuels would be required "for some years to come".
He argued there was a "rational" case for further exploration if the project's carbon emissions was lower than using imported fuel. 
The Scottish government, in its 2023 energy strategy, set out a presumption against new oil and gas drilling.
If passed by MPs, the UK government's Energy Independence Bill would remove the North Sea Transition Authority's ability to grant fresh oil and gas licences, in line with a Labour manifesto pledge not to grant permission for new fields.
It does not affect the decision on whether to allow drilling at Rosebank off Shetland - the UK's largest known untapped field - which was approved in 2022 before being subject to legal challenges.
Swinney has repeatedly refused to be drawn on whether he explicitly supports drilling at Rosebank. 







UK government to outlaw new North Sea drilling





Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm














Asked about the bill at First Minister's Questions, Swinney said: "The government has set out our view that because we are going to be using oil and gas for years to come there is a rational basis for considering oil and gas developments within our own jurisdiction if they offer lower carbon emissions than imported oil and gas."
He told parliament the UK government's bill includes several measures his government supports, adding: "But we do not support the provisions of that bill in relation to the position on the granting of new licences." 
Swinney said this was because "any particular applications need to be considered in relation to their impact on our carbon reduction target and given the fact we are going to be using oil and gas for some years to come". 
'Shocking U-turn' 
Decisions on new oil and gas licences are made by the UK government. 
However, under Nicola Sturgeon's leadership, the Scottish government proposed a presumption against new oil and gas developments. 
The Swinney administration appears to have shifted away from that position, especially since the outbreak of war in the Middle East. 
Scottish ministers nevertheless continue to stress any oil and gas developments should be compatible with the government's ambitions to cut carbon emissions over time.





Scottish Greens co-leader Gillian Mackay described Swinney's comments as a "shocking U-turn". 
She said: "It is a huge departure from only a few years ago when the Scottish government was committed to a presumption against oil and gas.
"When even the UK government is taking a stronger position, it shows how far the SNP has drifted. It is a shameful retreat and a slap in the face for future generations."

I am thinking of selling my car and buying a newer, smaller, more economical one. I have as much interest and expertise in cars as I do in thermo-nuclear engineering, or crypto currency, and so I have to ask advice from friends who know about motors. My first question is: should I go electric? To which the answer, without exception, is: no. 
I live in a fairly remote part of the countryside, so there is the matter of charging points, and the lack thereof. In addition, the limited battery range of the car might be a problem, and I’m told, the national infrastructure for electric vehicles isn’t quite up to speed yet. My urge to do something positive for the environment might have to wait. 
And then, thanks to the government, comes the killer blow. EV drivers don’t buy petrol and therefore don’t pay fuel duty, which has a rather inconvenient consequence for the country’s tax revenues. Fuel duty contributes around £25bn a year to the Treasury’s coffers, so unsurprisingly, the government is looking for ways that EV drivers can make up this particular shortfall.



 
Last week’s Budget was clear on the policy objective underpinning this. The small print in the Budget says: “As more people choose to switch to cleaner, greener electric cars … fuel duty receipts will decline. [The Electric Vehicle Excise Duty] is intended to help replace lost fuel duty revenue from cars over the long term so, like fuel duty, the amount motorists pay will vary based on the amount they drive.” 
It’s the final sentence that carries the punch. A mileage-based tax for electric vehicles, intended to be introduced in April 2028, might seem fair: EVs contribute just as much to the congestion and wear and tear on our roads, so why shouldn’t their drivers pay their share for the upkeep of our road network, based on usage? 
The difficulty comes with how this tax is calculated. The proposal is that EV drivers supply an estimate of the number of miles they intend to drive in a tax year, and they will then be charged a tax at 3p a mile. This voluntary scheme is clearly less than watertight, so buried in the Budget verbiage, is something of a provocative suggestion. The government would like to use the in-built internet and GPS tracking systems in newer EVs to interact with official databases in order to record the number of miles driven. 
This “in-built connectivity”, they say, would reduce tax fraud and make the process simpler and more accurate for both drivers and the Treasury. But what is actually being proposed is tracking each and every one of our journeys. The minute you leave your driveway, you are being watched.

Warming UK seas could ‘fundamentally reshape marine ecosystems’ – report



Four-year study warns destabilised marine food webs could jeopardise food security by 2050




Warming seas around the UK and the wider north-east Atlantic could destabilise marine food webs, weaken ocean health and jeopardise food security by 2050, according to a four-year study.
Scientists who projected the impact of climate breakdown on four key groups of marine life crucial to maintaining ocean ecosystems in the region said their results challenged assumptions that in middle latitudes, such as the UK, marine biodiversity was likely to increase across the board.

Instead, their projections highlight a predator-prey imbalance that could “fundamentally reshape marine ecosystems” in unforeseen ways, they said.
The seas around the British and Irish Isles, particularly the southern North Sea, have been identified as “marine climate hotspots”, one of 20 globally to have warmed the fastest over 50 years.
The new predictions, under a scenario of 3C (5.4F) of warming by 2100, found that while fish and seabed invertebrates may become more diverse by mid-century, key plankton groups lower in the food chain were likely to decline. This imbalance, the authors of the report said, could disrupt marine food webs and weaken the health and resilience of ocean ecosystems.
“What surprised us is that warming doesn’t increase or decrease biodiversity across the board,” said Elena Couce, a marine ecologist at the Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (Cefas), a British government agency, and co-lead author of the study.
“While some groups higher up the food chain, like fish, may gain species in parts of the north-east Atlantic, key plankton groups that underpin marine ecosystems are projected to lose species,” she said.
The research, led by Cefas and published in Science Advances, involved an international team of researchers from the University of East Anglia, the Marine Biological Association, UiT the Arctic University of Norway, the Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research and the Technical University of Denmark.

articles.title: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
articles.raw_rss: Even for countries where typhoons are a way of life, the last few months have brought unusually wild weather.
articles.raw_meta: Even for countries where typhoons are a way of life, the last few months have brought unusually wild weather.
articles.jina_text:
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.
A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.
In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.
Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.
It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.
In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.




Image source, VCG via Getty Images
Image caption, 

This riverside park in the south-eastern Chinese city of Nanning was submerged by Tropical Storm Narra




August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.








'Burning with fever'




The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.
El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.









The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in Septembe

Notable storms have included Typhoon Champi, which approached Taiwan with category five hurricane-equivalent winds, and Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days before striking eastern China.
